summary: Haiku research sweep of the academic + industry landscape around dawnr (verified-data LLMs, multi-prover specs, autoformalization), each source fetched to confirm it is real

findings.dimension: Autoformalization (natural-language math and specs to formal statements in Lean, Isabelle, Dafny)
findings.landscape: Autoformalization has moved from feasibility (Wu et al. 2022: LLMs translated 25.3% of competition problems perfectly into Isabelle/HOL) to a fidelity problem, and the 2025-26 evidence puts most failures in the statement rather than the proof: miniF2F's formal and informal statements disagree for more than half of its problems (corrected miniF2F-v2 raises full-pipeline accuracy from about 40% to 70%), and current techniques reach up to 45.1% on undergraduate mathematics (Poiroux et al., EMNLP 2025). Lean-side systems are now strong on competition math: StepFun-Formalizer-32B reports 40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, Herald's translator reports 93.2% pass@128 on miniF2F-test (but 22.5% on a graduate textbook set), Math Inc's Gauss agent reports a Lean formalization of the strong PNT of over 25k lines (self-reported, with humans reviewing key lemmas), and Axiom reports 12 of 12 Putnam 2025 problems in Lean (a company post that does not say who wrote the statements). The NL-to-verified-spec side lags far behind: vericoding finds off-the-shelf solve rates of 82% (Dafny), 44% (Verus) and 27% (Lean) for spec-to-code, VERINA's best model gets sound-and-complete specs 52.3% of the time with 4.9% proofs, and VerifyThisBench's strongest named model (o3-mini) passes under 4%. FormalRx (ICML 2026) and a Lean 4 paraphrase study (Apr 2026) show that errors cluster in semantic misalignment and in invalid Lean code, while my searches did not specifically cover F*, Rocq, Frama-C or SPARK.

key_works.title: Autoformalization with Large Language Models
key_works.what: Founding NL-to-statement result: LLMs translated 25.3% of competition problems perfectly into Isabelle/HOL, and the autoformalized theorems raised a neural prover's miniF2F rate from 29.6% to 35.2%.
key_works.who: Wu, Jiang, Li, Rabe, Staats, Jamnik, Szegedy (Google Research, Stanford, Cambridge)

key_works.title: Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
key_works.what: Proposes BEq+, an automated metric that correlates strongly with human judgment; ProofNetVerif (3,752 annotated examples) to validate metrics; ProofNet# (corrected ProofNet); RLM25 (619 research-level pairs from six formalization projects). Shows equivalence metrics need their own labeled validation set.

key_works.title: miniF2F-Lean Revisited: Reviewing Limitations and Charting a Path Forward
key_works.what: Formal and informal statements disagree for more than half of miniF2F problems; the corrected miniF2F-v2 (fully verified statements and proofs) raises best full-pipeline accuracy from about 40% to 70%. Unaudited benchmark statements can dominate reported gains.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.what: 12,504 formal specifications (Dafny 3,029; Verus/Rust 2,334; Lean 7,141). Off-the-shelf solve rates 82% Dafny, 44% Verus, 27% Lean; plain-English descriptions do not significantly help. The per-verifier spread is the risk for a seven-kernel gate.
key_works.who: Bursuc et al. (BAIF) with Chiosa, Zhao, Tan, Tegmark (MIT)

key_works.title: Can Large Language Models Transform Natural Language Intent into Formal Method Postconditions?
key_works.what: nl2postcond: generated postconditions caught 64 real-world Defects4J bugs and were judged generally correct and discriminating; the authors say it is unclear whether LLMs can match programmer intent. Closest prior art to the twin gate's discriminative test.

key_works.title: VERINA: Benchmarking Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.what: 189 manually curated Lean tasks scoring code, specification and proof separately. Fetched version: top model o3 reaches 72.6% code correctness, 52.3% sound-and-complete specs, 4.9% proof success (one trial per task); a search summary of an earlier version gave o4-mini at 61.4/51.0/3.6. The spec is the bottleneck.

key_works.title: VerifyThisBench: Generating Code, Specifications, and Proofs All at Once
key_works.what: End-to-end test from a natural-language description: extract a formal spec, implement it in a verification-aware language, produce a machine-checkable proof. Strongest named model (o3-mini) passes under 4%, with many outputs failing to compile.
key_works.who: Deng, Zhong, Bayazıt, Veneris, Long, Si

key_works.title: FormalRx: Rectify and eXamine Semantic Failures in Autoformalization
key_works.what: Diagnostic framework on the SCI Error Taxonomy: alignment verdict F1 0.88, error categorization F1 0.71, localization accuracy 0.75, correction accuracy 0.73; FormalRx-8B trained on 56,287 NL-FL pairs, with FormalRx-Test released. The most direct recent work on where statements go semantically wrong.
key_works.who: Wang, Huang, Wan, Zhu, Liu, Huang, Guo

key_works.title: Characterizing Paraphrase-Induced Failures in Lean 4 Autoformalization
key_works.what: Deterministic paraphrases of undergraduate and Olympiad problems across four frontier and three open-weight autoformalizers. Sensitivity is dominated by failures at the code-generation layer (invalid Lean); state-of-the-art autoformalizers still struggle to generate valid Lean. Compile-stage gating is a real failure mode.

key_works.title: Autoformalization in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey
key_works.what: Survey of the autoformalization workflow (data preprocessing, modeling, evaluation) from mathematical and LLM-centric views, framing formalization as a route to verifiable LLM outputs. Fetched abstract only.
key_works.who: Weng, Du, Li, Lu, Sun, Liu, Zhang

key_works.title: Herald: A Natural Language Annotated Lean 4 Dataset
key_works.what: Translates Mathlib4 into natural language to build parallel data; the Herald Translator formalizes NL statements in Lean: 93.2% pass@128 on miniF2F-test and 22.5% on an internal graduate textbook set (fetched version; a later version reports 96.7% and 23.5%, per search).
key_works.who: Gao, Wang, Jiang, Gao, Qin, Xu, Dong

key_works.title: StepFun-Formalizer: Unlocking the Autoformalization Potential of LLMs through Knowledge-Reasoning Fusion
key_works.what: ThinkingF data synthesis plus SFT and RLVR at 7B and 32B; the 32B model reaches BEq@1 40.5% on FormalMATH-Lite and 26.7% on ProverBench. The fetched abstract does not name the target language; baselines are in the full paper.

key_works.title: math-inc/strongpnt (Gauss autoformalization agent)
key_works.what: Repo states most statements and proofs in this over-25k-line, 1.1k-definition Lean formalization of the strong PNT were produced by the Gauss agent; humans wrote the blueprint and reviewed key lemmas. The three-week timing is self-reported. The largest end-to-end autoformalization claim: check it, do not cite it as independent.

key_works.title: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures
key_works.what: Lean statements of open conjectures (sources include Wikipedia, MathOverflow, OEIS, arXiv), community-written and human-reviewed. The README warns subtle inaccuracies can arise and plans to use AlphaProof to find misformalizations. A live audit target for statement faithfulness.

key_works.title: Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
key_works.what: Lemma-style whole-proof prover refining proofs with Lean feedback; fully proves 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems, 78.1% of formalized past IMO problems, and over 50% of PutnamBench. The abstract does not say who wrote the Lean statements.
key_works.who: Chen, Gu, et al. (ByteDance Seed per search)

key_works.title: Goedel-Prover-V2: Scaling Formal Theorem Proving with Scaffolded Data Synthesis and Self-Correction
key_works.what: 8B and 32B provers: 84.6% and 88.1% pass@32 on miniF2F (90.4% with self-correction); the flagship solves 86 PutnamBench problems at pass@184. Self-correction uses Lean compiler feedback; the abstract describes no statement-faithfulness check.
key_works.who: Lin, Tang, et al. (incl. Arora, Jin)

key_works.title: Aristotle: IMO-level Automated Theorem Proving
key_works.what: Pairs Lean proof search with an informal reasoner that produces and formalizes lemmas, plus a geometry solver; claims gold-medal-equivalent performance on the 2025 IMO. Affiliation and per-solution machine checking are not on the fetched page.
key_works.who: Harmonic (per search, not on fetched page)

key_works.title: AxiomProver at Putnam 2025
key_works.what: Company post: AxiomProver fully solved 12 of 12 Putnam 2025 problems in Lean, eight within the exam window, and describes the proofs as machine-checked. It does not say whether humans or the system wrote the Lean statements, which is the autoformalization question.

key_works.title: FormaTheoria: Constructing Large-Scale Lean Theories from Mathematical Literature
key_works.what: AI-assisted workflow building a coherent Lean theory from literature, reaching the Bender-Suzuki theorem in CFSG components (Feit-Thompson, Glauberman Z*, Brauer-Suzuki included). Names semantic fidelity and cross-source misalignment as challenges; the abstract gives no size counts and no fidelity test.
key_works.who: Nie, Zhang, Tang, Testa, Yau, Li, Zhou

key_works.title: AxDafny: Agentic Verified Code Generation in Dafny
key_works.what: Verifier-guided repair for Dafny: 92.7% verification success on DafnyBench, 6.5 points above the strongest proof-hint baseline; LCB-Pro-Dafny has 250 competition problems. Dafny is the easiest verifier target on the vericoding numbers; the NL-to-spec step is not covered.

key_works.title: PutnamBench: Evaluating Neural Theorem-Provers on the Putnam Mathematical Competition
key_works.what: Putnam 1962-2025 manually formalized in Lean 4 (672), Isabelle (640) and Coq (412): 1,724 formalizations in all. The fetched page links out to the leaderboard, which I did not capture; leaderboard snapshots seen in search are stale.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap, not novelty, on the core idea: autoformalization already names dawnr's central failure (a statement that compiles yet says the wrong thing; the miniF2F audit and FormalRx's error taxonomy), and nl2postcond (Endres et al., FSE 2024) already uses the same discriminative test, scoring generated postconditions by whether they catch real bugs (64 Defects4J bugs). The twin gate is that idea made stricter (seven independent kernels must agree and produce a concrete counterexample), so the defensible claim is the cross-kernel agreement and a measured gate, not mutation-based spec checking. Refutation-based screening is prior art in spirit too: a search snippet says FormalMATH disproves negations to filter statements (not confirmed by fetch). Confirmation: the miniF2F-v2 correction, the paraphrase study (failures cluster in code generation, not semantics), and the 2025 survey's claim that formalization makes LLM outputs verifiable all support dawnr's thesis and its honest-refusal rule, which fits FormalRx's move from binary verdicts to diagnosis. Threat: the NL-to-verified-spec benchmark niche is already crowded across Dafny, Verus and Lean (vericoding; VERINA and VerifyThisBench), so a claim to be the first multi-verifier spec benchmark would not survive review. None of the fetched papers reports agreement across seven independent kernels on one program, but my search was not exhaustive. Practical risk: the gate passes only when every kernel does, so the weakest kernel bounds yield, and vericoding's 55-point spread between Dafny (82%) and Lean (27%) suggests Lean or Verus will be the bottleneck.
opportunities: Report the gate's own false-accept rate. None of the autoformalization abstracts I fetched (Wu et al. 2022, Poiroux et al. 2025, Herald, StepFun-Formalizer, Seed-Prover, Goedel-Prover-V2) headlines an audited false-accept rate for a multi-check gate; they report accuracy against a reference or pass@k.

Per-kernel yield and disagreement. vericoding's Dafny-to-Lean spread (82% vs 27%) means the weakest kernel bounds a seven-kernel gate; publish verify and refute rates per kernel, and map which kernels disagree onto FormalRx's error categories.

Coverage-versus-accuracy curves for honest refusal. The fetched results report accuracy on attempted items only; a selective-prediction curve for the t gate (coverage against audited accuracy) is a metric none of the fetched abstracts reports.

A labeled faithfulness set built from gate decisions. ProofNetVerif (3,752 annotated examples) validates Lean equivalence metrics; I found no comparable labeled set for NL-to-verified-spec across several languages, and audited t decisions could become one.

Spec as the audited artifact. vericoding and VERINA headline verified-code success, while VERINA's specs and proofs separate sharply (52.3% sound-and-complete specs against 4.9% proofs); scoring specs under a mutation gate targets the measured bottleneck rather than proof search.

Re-audit shared statement corpora with the twin gate. miniF2F (more than half mismatched) and formal-conjectures (which warns that subtle inaccuracies can arise) show public statements are unreliable; a twin-checked re-audit of one such set would be a publishable contribution.

Non-Lean targets, to verify first. The NL-to-statement systems I fetched are Lean-centric (Herald, Gauss, Seed-Prover, Goedel-Prover-V2) and the Isabelle anchor is Wu et al. 2022; my searches did not cover F*, Rocq, Frama-C or SPARK, so check before claiming an empty niche there, where the seven-kernel setup is unusual.
findings.direction_hint: Turn the twin gate into a measured autoformalization study: on about 200 NL problems, run the t pipeline with and without the twin check, hand-audit a random sample of accepted specs against the NL statement, and publish the gate's false-accept rate with its coverage curve. This uses data dawnr already produces and reports the quantity that the miniF2F-v2 and ProofNetVerif work show is missing from most reported results.

findings.dimension: LLM / neural theorem proving and proof synthesis (Lean, Isabelle, Coq/Rocq, Dafny, Verus)
findings.landscape: Lean provers now reach large shares of the benchmark frontier through RL and self-play on machine-checked data: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 reports 88.9% on MiniF2F-test at 671B and 49 of 658 PutnamBench (2025), Goedel-Prover-V2 reports 84.6% pass@32 at 8B and says that beats the 671B model at pass@32 (ICLR 2026), Seed-Prover claims over half of PutnamBench and 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems, and AlphaProof (Nature 2025) solved 3 of 5 non-geometry IMO 2024 problems after training on millions of auto-formalized statements. The verified training data is mostly generated or auto-formalized statements, with self-play (STP: 28.5% vs 13.2% of LeanWorkbook) and scaffolded difficulty as the yield levers, plus LeanDojo's 98,734 theorems mined from Mathlib, while outside Lean the same tasks are much harder: off-the-shelf models solve about 82% of Dafny, 44% of Verus and 27% of Lean in the Vericoding benchmark (12,504 specs), and AlgoVeri's identical contracts give 40.3% on Dafny (Gemini-3 Flash), 24.7% on Verus and 7.8% on Lean. The main 2026 correction is that a checker accepts the formal statement, not the intent: the "Faults" audit (ICML 2026) found 4,833 issues across five Lean benchmarks and their forks, 398 of them mechanically certified as counterexamples, vacuous theorems or unsound axioms. Unconfirmed 2026 vendor claims put PutnamBench at 587 of 672 (Mistral Leanstral 1.5) and 672 of 672 (NEAR AI), with Axiom's AxiomProver reporting 12 of 12 Putnam 2025 in Lean on its primary page; I could not search SPARK/Ada or F* because the session search budget ran out, so those two targets are unchecked.

key_works.title: Goedel-Prover-V2: Scaling Formal Theorem Proving with Scaffolded Data Synthesis and Self-Correction
key_works.what: Scaffolded synthetic tasks of rising difficulty plus Lean-compiler self-correction. The 8B model scores 84.6% pass@32 on MiniF2F, which the paper says beats the 671B DeepSeek-Prover-V2 at pass@32; the 32B scores 88.1% (90.4% with self-correction) and solves 86 PutnamBench problems at pass@184. The strongest per-parameter data point for dawnr's thesis, but on pretrained bases and proof-search metrics.

key_works.title: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 (Advancing Formal Mathematical Reasoning via RL for Subgoal Decomposition)
key_works.what: Cold start where DeepSeek-V3 decomposes hard statements into subgoals and solved subgoal proofs are stitched into chains, followed by RL. The abstract reports 88.9% on MiniF2F-test at 671B (sampling budget not stated) and 49 of 658 PutnamBench (Goedel-Prover-V2 cites 47 at pass@1024). The baseline the small-model claims are measured against.

key_works.title: Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
key_works.what: Lemma-style whole-proof Lean prover that refines using Lean feedback, previously proved lemmas and self-summaries. Authors claim over half of PutnamBench, 78.1% of past formalized IMO problems, and 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems fully proven (no counts on the abstract page).

key_works.title: Olympiad-Level Formal Mathematical Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning (AlphaProof)
key_works.what: AlphaZero-style RL on millions of auto-formalized Lean statements. Solved 3 of 5 non-geometry IMO 2024 problems, silver-level with AlphaGeometry 2; Test-Time RL generates problem variants at inference for the hardest problems. The page states no limitations and stresses that other systems lack the formal verification needed to guarantee correctness.

key_works.title: STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
key_works.what: Self-play in which a conjecturer and a prover train each other: the conjecturer is rewarded for statements barely provable by the current prover, and proving uses expert iteration. Reports 28.5% of LeanWorkbook against 13.2% for expert iteration. Verifier-scored self-play is the data-generation baseline any generated-corpus claim must beat.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.what: 12,504 formal specifications (3,029 Dafny, 2,334 Verus, 7,141 Lean; 6,174 unseen). Off-the-shelf LLMs solve about 82% of Dafny, 44% of Verus and 27% of Lean tasks. The abstract describes no specification-adequacy check, so a twin-style audit is unaddressed here.

key_works.title: AlgoVeri: An Aligned Benchmark for Verified Code Generation on Classical Algorithms
key_works.what: 77 classical algorithms with identical functional contracts in Dafny, Verus and Lean. Gemini-3 Flash reaches 40.3% on Dafny, 24.7% on Verus and 7.8% on Lean (model not named for the last two), and the authors argue per-language suites cannot be compared. The closest prior art to dawnr's one-source, many-kernel design; the abstract describes no mutation or adequacy check.

key_works.title: Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking: Dataset Defects and Evaluation Failures in Lean Theorem Proving
key_works.what: Audit of five widely used Lean benchmarks and their forks: 4,833 findings, 398 mechanically certified (counterexamples, vacuous theorems, unsound axioms), plus semantic defects (missing hypotheses, simplified problems, incorrect translations). States the kernel does not verify that the statement faithfully encodes the intended informal problem, and releases checkers and corrected snapshots. The direct evidence that acceptance is not intent.

key_works.title: AlphaVerus: Bootstrapping Formally Verified Code Generation through Self-Improving Translation and Treefinement
key_works.what: Inference-time, with no fine-tuning or human intervention: translates Dafny programs into Verus, then tree-search refinement guided by verifier output, filtering misaligned specifications to prevent reward hacking. That is the weak-spec failure dawnr's twin targets. Uses Llama-3.1-70B; the abstract gives no success figure.

key_works.title: AutoVerus: Automated Proof Generation for Rust Code
key_works.what: Multi-agent Verus proof generation mirroring expert stages (attempt, refine with hints, debug with verifier errors). Authors report over 90% of a 150-task benchmark, with over half solved in under 30 seconds or three LLM calls. Own results, not independently replicated; the abstract page does not state whether models were fine-tuned.

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.what: Checks consistency among code, docstring and Dafny annotations: up to 87% acceptance of correct CloverBench programs, zero false positives on incorrect ones (authors' claim), and six faulty programs found in MBPP-DFY-50. The nearest prior art for spec-adequacy checks, though it is consistency-based and the benchmark is textbook-level.

key_works.title: Cobblestone (Coq proof synthesis, arXiv 2410.19940)
key_works.what: Divide-and-conquer Coq proof search: an unsound LLM proposes candidate proofs, verified parts are kept and the rest retried. The abstract claims a guaranteed-sound output despite the reliance on unsound LLMs. Averages $1.25 and 14.7 minutes per run; up to 58% of theorems with a supplied proof structure. A clean statement of the checker-not-generator trust model.

key_works.title: Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with Large Language Models
key_works.what: Whole-proof generation plus repair, where the repair model sees the failed proof and its error message. On 6,336 Isabelle/HOL theorems it adds 8.7% over Thor, and Baldur plus Thor reach 65.7% without manual intervention. Early evidence that verifier error feedback is the repair signal.

key_works.title: LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
key_works.what: Open Lean toolkit and a dataset of 98,734 theorems extracted from Lean's math library, with ReProver, a retrieval-augmented prover that the abstract says needs one GPU week of training and beats non-retrieval baselines and GPT-4 (no figures on the page). The open Lean data and retrieval baseline.

key_works.title: From seeing why to checking everything (AxiomProver at Putnam 2025)
key_works.what: Claims AxiomProver fully solved 12 of 12 Putnam 2025 problems in Lean, 8 within the exam window; the A5 formalization is 2,054 lines and took 518 minutes, and a technical report is promised. The page does not address whether the formal statements match the originals, so it shows proof power, not faithfulness. A vendor claim.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap and prior art: the loop at dawnr's core, where only kernel-accepted outputs become training data, is established rather than novel. DeepSeek-Prover-V2, Goedel-Prover-V2, Seed-Prover, AlphaProof and STP all use the checker's accept or reject as the success signal, and AlphaProof's page stresses that other systems lack the formal verification needed to guarantee correctness. The per-parameter thesis already has a Lean instance: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B is reported to beat DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B at pass@32 on MiniF2F, which supports dawnr's direction for proof search. That evidence is not dawnr's experiment, though: those are pretrained large bases scored on proof success, not a from-scratch small model compared with a raw-code control at matched tokens, so that comparison remains untested in this literature. Confirmation of the honest-refusal rule: the 2026 Faults audit shows acceptance is not intent, and its counterexample, vacuous-theorem and unsound-axiom categories are what a refutation gate should refuse. Cobblestone's claim of a sound output from an unsound generator is the same trust model (trust the checker, not the generator). Threats: the verify-then-train flywheel must be cited, not claimed; inference-time verifier search already works on Verus (AutoVerus reports over 90% on its own 150 tasks, authors' claim) and Coq (Cobblestone), so the scarce resource is correct specifications rather than proofs; and the 7-of-7 bar may starve the data, since Lean is the weakest target (27% in Vericoding, 7.8% in AlgoVeri), so per-kernel yield has to be measured or the strictest gate becomes the bottleneck. The closest prior art to dawnr's one-source, many-kernel design is AlgoVeri, and its abstract describes no adequacy or mutation check, which is where dawnr differs.
opportunities: Publish a twin-survival audit: run dawnr's one-edit refutation over the Vericoding specifications (12,504), AlgoVeri's 77 algorithms in three languages, and the Lean benchmarks audited in Faults, and report mutant-survival rates by defect class. It needs no training, is mechanical rather than an LLM judgment, and addresses a 2026 open problem.

Cross-kernel disagreement as a result: in the papers read, no system requires agreement across independent checkers for one artifact (Lean in DeepSeek, Goedel, Seed, AlphaProof and LeanDojo; Isabelle in Baldur; Dafny in Clover; Verus in AlphaVerus and AutoVerus; Coq in Cobblestone). A taxonomy of which kernel rejects what, and why, across the seven targets would be new data.

Fixed-budget, verdict-honest reporting: prover results compare different k (Goedel's 86 at pass@184 against DeepSeek's 47 at pass@1024), and AlgoVeri says per-language scores are not comparable. dawnr can report accepted-but-refuted rate, refusal rate and cost per verified program at one stated budget, which none of the papers read reports.

Matched-compute, from-scratch control: the prover papers train or search over pretrained large models and score proof success. No paper read trains a small from-scratch model on kernel-verified programs against a raw-code control at matched tokens, so dawnr's central experiment is an open slot.

Per-kernel yield and curriculum: with Lean at 27% (Vericoding) and 7.8% (AlgoVeri), a study that orders kernels from easy to hard and reports how much data the 7-of-7 gate keeps would show whether the strict bar is affordable.

Twin as a filter for generated corpora: STP's conjecturer is rewarded for statements barely provable by the prover (28.5% vs 13.2%). A twin-refuted, verifier-accepted generated program is a candidate filter against trivially true generated statements, a risk any self-play generator faces.

SPARK/Ada and F*: no LLM proof-synthesis work for either surfaced in the searches I completed, but the dedicated searches were blocked by the session budget, so treat this gap as unverified. Frama-C has some LLM spec-synthesis work (AutoACSL, search snippet only, not fetched).
findings.direction_hint: Before any new training or proof-rate push, turn the twin gate into a published adequacy audit: run one-edit refutation over the Vericoding and AlgoVeri specifications and over dawnr's own verified set, report mutant-survival rates by defect class, and release the checker.

findings.dimension: RLVR for reasoning and code: verifier and test-suite rewards, outcome vs process rewards, reward hacking (2024-2026)
findings.landscape: RLVR became the default post-training recipe in 2024-2025: Tulu 3 (Ai2 and UW, Nov 2024) named it as RL on verifiable rewards with no reward model, and DeepSeek-R1 (Jan 2025) trained reasoning with GRPO on rule-based rewards, scoring code by compiler-run test cases and dropping neural reward models because of reward hacking. The same binary verifier reward moved into formal proof RL: DeepSeek-Prover-V2 (Apr 2025) trains Lean proofs with a 1/0 checker reward, while Dafny RL work (Re:Form, Jul 2025, and a 2026 master's thesis) found that verifier-only rewards get gamed by weak specifications and answered it with a ground-truth strength check or by filtering underspecified tasks. A skeptical line (NeurIPS 2025 oral, arXiv 2504.13837) finds RLVR mostly sharpens pass@1 and reweights paths the base model already has, while search-only 2025-2026 papers add reward-hacking detectors and show that answer-matching verifiers accept flawed derivations. Verus was searched and yielded only SFT-style data work (VeruSyn, Feb 2026, search only) and no RL paper; SPARK/Ada, Frama-C, F* and Rocq were not searched in this run.

key_works.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
key_works.what: GRPO with rule-based rewards (accuracy checks, with code scored by compiler-run predefined tests, plus a format reward). The paper says a neural reward model may suffer from reward hacking at scale, so R1-Zero used no neural reward model or PRM; R1's general-data stage did use reward models. Reported: R1-Zero AIME 2024 71.0 percent (86.7 with cons@64), R1 79.8 percent, R1 LiveCodeBench 65.9 percent.

key_works.title: Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training
key_works.what: Names RLVR: an RL stage trained on verifiable rewards instead of a reward model, rewarded only when the output verifies as correct, applied to math (GSM8K, MATH) and precise instruction following (IFEval). Gains are stage-level, not isolated RLVR ablations (8B: MATH 42.0 to 43.7, IFEval 81.1 to 82.4, DPO checkpoint to final), and section 8.1 headings list online DPO and rejection sampling among methods that did not reliably help. Read: first 100k of 246k characters plus abstract; RL algorithm not confirmed.

key_works.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
key_works.what: Across six popular RLVR algorithms, RL-trained models lead at pass@1, but base models reach higher pass@k at large k; the authors read RLVR as reweighting paths the base model already has, and say distillation from a teacher, unlike RLVR, can add new reasoning patterns. Listed as a NeurIPS 2025 oral.

key_works.title: Re:Form: Reducing Human Annotations in Scalable Formal Software Verification with RL in LLMs: A Preliminary Study on Dafny
key_works.what: GRPO on Dafny with three rule-based parts: spec compiles, Dafny verifier accepts, and the spec is at least as strong as a ground-truth spec (checked by two implications). The verification-only reward let the model exploit the verifier by issuing weak specifications that trivially satisfy it. The 14B RL model reaches 14.0 percent pass@1 on out-of-domain DafnyComp vs 8.3 percent for 14B SFT; the authors note the verifier is incomplete and entropy regularization unstable. key_works.title: Automating Formal Verification with Reinforcement Learning and Recursive Inference
key_works.what: RL on Dafny with compiler and verifier outcomes, plus a verifier-guided search scaffold in Lean. Defines specification hacking as models exploiting weak formal specifications instead of implementing the intended solution; mitigated by filtering underspecified or vulnerable tasks. Verified reward 2.2% to 58.1% (APPS-derived Dafny set); verified success 9.7% to 31.1% after multi-turn RLVR on a refined set. No twin or mutation check in the abstract. findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap: dawnr's acceptance rule (all seven kernels verify the real program and refute the one-edit twin) is a binary verifier reward of the same family as DeepSeek-R1's rule-based rewards, Tulu 3's RLVR and DeepSeek-Prover-V2's Lean reward. dawnr uses that reward today to filter SFT rows, not to drive RL, so RLVR as a technique is not dawnr's contribution; these papers bear on whether to add RL later and on what the reward must look like. Confirmation: Re:Form and the 2026 thesis independently find that a verifier-only reward is gamed by weak specifications, which is the failure the twin gate exists to catch, so dawnr's anti-hacking design has outside support. Threat and prior art: a verifier-rewarded RL loop for formal code is no longer novel in Lean or Dafny, and a must-be-rejected negative control (the contradictory test in arXiv 2604.23488, search only) is a known pattern, so dawnr's originality has to rest on being reference-free (Re:Form's subset reward needs a ground-truth spec; the twin needs none), cross-kernel (seven independent checkers rather than one), and measured per kernel. Caution for the research question: Tulu 3's section 8.1 headings list rejection sampling among methods that did not reliably help, and the pass@k paper argues RL mostly reweights, so any claim that verified-data training helps must be separated from any RL effect with a matched SFT control.

A reward that pays for honest refusal: every fetched recipe uses a binary correct-or-not reward, so none rewards a verified refusal above an unverified answer, which is the rule dawnr already states (an honest refusal beats a false verdict).
Per-kernel gaming and disagreement rates reported beside pass@k: the fetched text reports pass@k and verified-success numbers, but not which checker was gamed or how often a kernel disagreed.

A matched control at fixed parameters: the same verified rows trained as rejection-sampled SFT, as GRPO on the seven-kernel reward, and as raw-code SFT. The RLVR papers were not built to answer dawnr's per-parameter question.

findings.dimension: Training on execution-verified or rejection-sampled data: STaR, RFT, ReST, CodeRL, and verifier-filtered synthetic data (2022-2026)
findings.landscape: Checker-filtered self-training is a standard recipe: STaR (2022), ReST-EM and RFT (2023) sample, keep what a checker accepts, and fine-tune, and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) pairs rule-based RL rewards with about 600k rejection-sampled reasoning SFT examples, giving its Qwen-7B distill 55.5% on AIME 2024 and 92.8% on MATH-500. In formal and code settings the same loop yields small strong models: Goedel-Prover-V2 (2025) has an 8B Lean prover beating the 671B DeepSeek-Prover-V2 at pass@32 on MiniF2F, and ATLAS (Dec 2025) builds about 2,700 verified Dafny programs that lift a 7B model's DafnySynthesis Pass@5 from 15.8 to 65.8. The closest per-parameter evidence compares checker-filtered self-generated data with human data (RFT lifts LLaMA-7B on GSM8K from 35.9 to 49.3), not with unfiltered self-generated data, and a Sept 2025 paper argues strict test-based filtering discards valid diverse solutions, so whether the checker or the diversity drives the gain is still open.

key_works.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
key_works.what: Generate rationales, keep those reaching the correct answer, rationalize misses with the answer as a hint, retrain, repeat; abstract says it matches fine-tuning a 30x larger LM on CommonsenseQA. The origin of the loop dawnr runs.

key_works.title: Beyond Human Data: Scaling Self-Training for Problem-Solving with Language Models
key_works.what: EM-style loop: sample, keep what a binary checker marks correct, fine-tune, repeat; PaLM-2 on MATH and APPS; abstract says it scales with model size and significantly beats fine-tuning on human data alone. Direct precedent for checker-filtered code training.

key_works.title: Scaling Relationship on Learning Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models (RFT)
key_works.what: Keeps correct reasoning paths from SFT models as extra training data; LLaMA-7B on GSM8K goes from 35.9% (SFT) to 49.3% with pooled multi-model rejection samples; abstract ties larger gains to more distinct correct paths.

key_works.title: CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation through Pretrained Models and Deep Reinforcement Learning
key_works.what: Actor-critic for code: a pretrained code LM is the actor and a critic is trained to predict functional correctness and give dense feedback; at inference, critical sampling regenerates programs from unit-test feedback and critic scores; new SOTA on APPS.

key_works.title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
key_works.what: Samples very many programs and filters by program behavior down to a small submission set; abstract reports a top 54.3% ranking in contests with over 5,000 participants. Large-scale execution-filtering precedent.

key_works.title: V-STaR: Training Verifiers for Self-Taught Reasoners
key_works.what: Generator fine-tuned on self-generated solutions; DPO verifier trained on both correct and incorrect solutions and used to select among candidates at inference; 4 to 17% test-accuracy gains over prior self-improvement and verification methods on LLaMA-2 (code and math).

key_works.title: rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
key_works.what: Code-augmented MCTS rollouts yield step-level verified trajectories; four self-evolution rounds over 747k problems; Qwen2.5-Math-7B MATH 58.8% to 90.0%, Phi-3-mini-3.8B 41.4% to 86.4%, AIME average 53.3% (8 of 15).

key_works.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
key_works.what: Rule-based accuracy and format rewards in RL; about 600k reasoning SFT samples rejection-sampled from the RL checkpoint (rule-based checks where possible, a DeepSeek-V3 judge otherwise); distilled Qwen-7B scores 55.5% on AIME 2024 and 92.8% on MATH-500.

key_works.title: AlphaVerus: Bootstrapping Formally Verified Code Generation through Self-Improving Translation and Treefinement
key_works.what: Translates programs from a higher-resource language into Verus, guided by verifier feedback via Treefinement tree search, with a filter for misaligned specifications and programs to block reward hacking; Llama-3.1-70B; no model fine-tuning.

key_works.title: ATLAS: Automated Toolkit for Large-Scale Verified Code Synthesis
key_works.what: Synthesizes Dafny programs checked by the Dafny verifier from TACO contest problems (about 2.7K verified programs, 19,385 SFT examples); Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with LoRA: DafnyBench Pass@1 31.8% to 55.8%, DafnySynthesis Pass@5 15.8% to 65.8%; no raw-data control.

key_works.title: Goedel-Prover-V2: Scaling Formal Theorem Proving with Scaffolded Data Synthesis and Self-Correction
key_works.what: Expert iteration plus RL with scaffolded synthetic tasks, Lean-compiler self-correction and checkpoint averaging; 8B reaches 84.6% on MiniF2F pass@32, above DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B on the same metric; 32B reaches 88.1% (90.4% with self-correction).

key_works.title: MutDafny: A Mutation-Based Approach to Assess Dafny Specifications
key_works.what: Mutation testing for Dafny specifications with 40 operators; a mutant that still verifies flags a possibly weak spec; five weak specs found across 794 programs; used to assess specs, not to filter training data.

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.what: Consistency check across code, docstrings and formal annotations used as an acceptance filter: up to 87% acceptance on correct CloverBench instances and no false positives on adversarial incorrect ones (abstract); no fine-tuning.

key_works.title: Textbooks Are All You Need
key_works.what: 1.3B model trained on about 6B tokens of web code filtered for textbook quality plus about 1B GPT-3.5 textbook and exercise tokens; 50.6% HumanEval pass@1 and 55.5% MBPP; the abstract page has no matched-size filter ablation.

key_works.title: Verification Limits Code LLM Training
key_works.what: Argues test-based verification is too rigid: richer test suites give about +3 pass@1, relaxed thresholds or LLM soft verification +2 to 4 pass@1, and keeping diverse correct solutions per problem gives generalization gains; no unfiltered arm on the abstract page.

key_works.title: LLM-Based FORM Code Generation with Verification-Driven Fine-Tuning
key_works.what: Uses the FORM symbolic-algebra binary as an execution oracle to validate 4,633 training examples for Qwen3-8B with QLoRA; abstract says the specialist beats frontier models up to 756B on larger benchmarks; verified-vs-unverified arms are not on the abstract page. Closest niche analog to dawnr.

key_works.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
key_works.what: Coverage grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples; with an automatic verifier, SWE-bench Lite rises from 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples) for DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct; majority vote and reward models plateau without one. Inference-time only.

key_works.title: OpenThoughts: Data Recipes for Reasoning Models
key_works.what: Over 1,000 controlled data-recipe experiments; 1.2M examples with QwQ-32B traces; OpenThinker3-7B reaches 53% AIME 2025, 51% LiveCodeBench and 54% GPQA Diamond; the abstract does not isolate the effect of filtering. A template for a controlled ablation at 7B scale.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap, not novelty: dawnr's loop (sample t answers, keep those that pass the tests and where all seven provers verify and the twin is refuted, then fine-tune a small from-scratch model on the survivors) is STaR, ReST-EM and RFT over a formal target, and R1 distillation runs the same loop at larger scale, so the loop itself should not be claimed. Confirmation: rStar-Math, Goedel-Prover-V2, ATLAS and the R1 distills show checker-filtered data lifting small models in math and formal settings, so the premise is plausible. Threat: an all-seven plus twin-refutation admission rule is stricter than the admission rules in the works fetched, and 2509.20837 and RFT both point at distinct correct solutions as the source of value; if data is the binding constraint, a stricter filter can shrink the dataset and reduce its diversity, so the raw baseline could win for reasons unrelated to proof. Gates have prior art: MutDafny treats a surviving mutant as a weak-spec signal, Clover uses a consistency check as an acceptance filter, and AlphaVerus filters misaligned specifications to block reward hacking; the twin refutation is a known adequacy idea, and what I did not find is its use as a training-data admission rule across several provers. Inference-time side: LLM Monkeys finds coverage grows log-linearly with samples when an automatic verifier exists, which is the regime dawnr's checkers provide, so the offline-assistant direction is better supported than the training claim. Caveats: most fetches returned abstract pages, so figures are abstract-level, and the searches were not exhaustive. Unfetched leads to check before citing: Lean Workbook (NeurIPS 2024), KodCode (ACL 2025), the vericoding benchmark (arXiv 2509.22908), and a Guha et al. 2025 result, cited inside 2509.20837 and reported by a search snippet, that LLM-written unit-test filtering gave no gain over unfiltered data.
opportunities: Matched-diversity raw-vs-verified control: same problems, token budget and distinct solutions per problem, 3 seeds, scored on a held-out panel. None of the verified-data papers fetched runs it: ReST-EM compares against human data, ATLAS against its base model, and Goedel-Prover-V2 against other provers.

Graded admission arm: accept when k of 7 kernels verify and the twin is refuted, and compare with all seven, to measure what strictness costs in yield and diversity. 2509.20837 concerns test-based verification, so carrying its finding over to proofs is a hypothesis to test, not a result.

Per-kernel marginal value: retrain with admission filters built from 1, 3 and 7 provers, and with the twin gate on and off. In what I searched and read I found no multi-verifier training ablation, which makes this the most likely original measurement.

Refutation witnesses as exact negatives: each twin comes with a concrete refuting input, so (program, twin, witness) triples can train a verdict model. V-STaR reports 4 to 17% gains over prior self-improvement methods using a DPO verifier trained on correct and incorrect solutions, but its labels come from tests, not formal witnesses.

Refusal as a trained class: label problems where every sample was rejected as refuse, and report refusal precision and coverage together. None of the works fetched trains refusal from verifier outcomes, which fits dawnr's rule that an honest refusal beats a false verdict.
findings.direction_hint: Run the matched-diversity ablation before scaling data: at equal token budget and 3 seeds, compare raw tests-only t answers, all-seven verified answers and graded k-of-7 admission, with distinct solutions per problem matched across arms, and report whichever way it lands, since it decides whether dawnr's claim is about verification or about diversity.

findings.dimension: Prior art for one specification lowered to many provers (Why3, Boogie, Viper, intermediate verification languages, SMT portfolios), and how dawnr-t's seven kernels plus twin refutation differ
findings.landscape: Lowering one spec to several provers is established: Why3 sends WhyML verification conditions to SMT solvers (Alt-Ergo, CVC4/cvc5, Z3) and proof assistants (Rocq, PVS, Isabelle/HOL), with about 21 named provers on its site; Frama-C WP recommends Alt-Ergo, Coq, Z3 and CVC4 plus any other Why3 prover; SPARK's GNATprove detects and uses Z3, cvc5 and Alt-Ergo over an AdaCore fork of Why3. The 2024-2026 frontier is Rust-to-many-provers: Aeneas translates Charon's LLBC into F*, Coq, HOL4 and Lean (Lean and HOL4 described as most mature), hax targets F* (stable), Lean via Aeneas (active development) and Rocq, ProVerif, SSProve and EasyCrypt (experimental), and Creusot compiles Rust MIR to WhyML for Why3. Intermediate verification languages act as shared-solver hubs: Boogie, which Dafny is built on, defaults to Z3 (cvc5 and Yices2 experimental), and Viper has Silicon (symbolic execution, Z3 required) and Carbon (VC generation, needs Z3 and Boogie). The mutation-based spec-adequacy entry I found is MutDafny (arXiv 2511.15403, 2025), which treats a mutant that still verifies as a sign of a weak spec and found five weak specs across 794 Dafny programs. Coverage caveat: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after nine successful queries, so this rests on the official pages fetched here, not a full literature sweep.

key_works.title: Why3 platform (paper: Filliatre and Paskevich, 'Why3 - Where Programs Meet Provers', ESOP 2013)
key_works.what: WhyML programs produce verification conditions sent to external provers: SMT (Alt-Ergo, CVC4/cvc5, Z3) and interactive (Rocq, PVS, Isabelle/HOL), about 21 named on the site. The closest precedent for one spec, many provers, with one VC layer feeding all of them. The ESOP paper itself was seen only in search results.

key_works.title: Boogie intermediate verification language
key_works.what: Described as a modeling language intended as a layer on which to build program verifiers for other languages. Default solver is Z3, with cvc5 and Yices2 experimental; Dafny is built on it, so Dafny's kernel inherits the Z3 default. The IVL-hub pattern.

key_works.title: Silicon (Viper's default verifier)
key_works.what: Symbolic-execution verifier and default backend for the Viper intermediate language. Requires Z3, with cvc5 as an optional second solver. One IVL with two verifiers, both on SMT.

key_works.title: Carbon (second Viper verifier)
key_works.what: Verification-condition-generation verifier for Viper. Setup requires Z3 and Boogie, though the page does not state the Boogie target outright. Shows redundancy inside one IVL with a shared solver.

key_works.title: Aeneas: Rust Verification by Functional Translation (ICFP 2022)
key_works.what: Charon's LLBC from Rust is translated to pure lambda calculus with backends F*, Coq, HOL4 and Lean (HOL4 and Lean called most mature; Isabelle not yet a backend). One source into several proof assistants, but the README describes no adequacy or refutation gate.

key_works.title: hax (Cryspen): Rust to F*, Rocq, Lean and others
key_works.what: Backend table: F* stable; Lean via Aeneas in active development; Rocq/Coq, ProVerif, SSProve and EasyCrypt experimental. The most explicit maturity-labelled multi-target lowering found, and uneven target maturity is the risk an all-kernels rule must handle.

key_works.title: hax: Verifying Security-Critical Rust Software using Multiple Provers (IACR ePrint 2025/142)
key_works.who: Bhargavan, Buyse, Franceschino, Kiefer, Schneider-Bensch (Cryspen); Hansen, Spitters (Aarhus University)
key_works.what: The 2025 academic statement of the same multi-prover idea: one Rust input, several proof backends, with ProVerif, SSProve, Coq and F* named on the page. The closest 2025 comparator to dawnr's approach.

key_works.title: Creusot architecture (Rust to Why3)
key_works.what: Rust MIR is translated to WhyML (one Why module per function) and discharged through Why3. The page does not name the provers or mention Rocq. Another Rust route into the same Why3 VC layer.

key_works.title: Frama-C WP plugin: prover list
key_works.what: WP recommends Alt-Ergo, Coq, Z3 and CVC4 plus all other provers Why3 supports, with an internal prover Qed that simplifies obligations before they go to external provers. So one C/ACSL spec already reaches a proof assistant and SMT solvers, and the page implies a Why3 route. Overlaps dawnr's Frama-C kernel directly.

key_works.title: SPARK2014 / GNATprove
key_works.what: GNATprove detects and uses Z3, cvc5 and Alt-Ergo from PATH and builds on an AdaCore fork of Why3 as a submodule. The README does not mention Coq or Rocq. The SPARK portfolio is SMT-based and sits on Why3, the layer Frama-C WP can also reach.

key_works.title: Verus user guide (Rust verifier)
key_works.what: The guide says proofs are aided by Z3; the README only says Verus relies on powerful solvers. An SMT-backed Rust kernel in dawnr's set that shares the Z3 risk.

key_works.title: MutDafny: a mutation-based approach to assess Dafny specifications (arXiv 2511.15403)
key_works.what: Injects faults into Dafny code across 794 real-world programs; a mutant that still verifies may indicate a weak spec, and manual analysis of undetected mutants found five weak specs. The closest mutation prior art to the twin gate, but Dafny-only, uses verification as the oracle, and the abstract describes no refutation at a concrete input.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Unoriginal parts: writing one spec and discharging it with several provers is established (Why3, Frama-C WP, SPARK, Aeneas, hax), so dawnr should not present that as new. Confirmation: hax's own backend table labels four of its six targets experimental, so uniform semantics across provers is hard, which supports a gate like dawnr's. Threat to the independence claim: Z3 is the default or a listed solver in the docs of four of dawnr's seven kernels (Boogie under Dafny, Verus per its guide, SPARK's GNATprove, Frama-C WP), and SPARK's GNATprove sits on Why3 while Frama-C WP can reach Why3's provers, so one Z3 or Why3 fault could reach several kernels at once. F* was not confirmed in this run, and the sources here do not place Lean or Rocq on Z3 or Why3. Difference: Why3-style systems push every prover through one WhyML verification-condition layer, while dawnr's 'seven independent proof systems' description implies a separate lowering per kernel; that difference only counts if the lowerings really share no code path. Closest to original is the twin gate: MutDafny uses surviving mutants as a weak-spec signal, but only for Dafny and without a concrete-input refutation, and no fetched source requires every backend to agree or refutes a one-edit twin across several provers.

findings.dimension: Mutation testing, metamorphic and differential testing, and specification adequacy (vacuity, assertion strength): dawnr's twin-refutation gate
findings.landscape: Mutation-based checking of formal specifications became a concrete research line for Dafny and JML in 2024-2026. IronSpec (OSDI 2024) adds automated spec mutation testing to sanity checks and found ten spec bugs across six real verified systems, and MutDafny (ICSE 2026) reverses the direction: it mutates 794 real Dafny programs with 40 operators and uses the specs as detectors, which surfaced five weak real specs. Spec-Harness (arXiv 2604.00280, 2026, JML) reports that 22.7% of verifier-approved specs have no postcondition at all, so verifier acceptance is not adequacy evidence, while nl2postcond (FSE 2024) and Beyond Postconditions (arXiv 2510.12702) grade LLM-written contracts by discriminative power and verifier soundness. Containment Verification (arXiv 2605.09045, 2026) says its LLM-written Dafny specs are produced under an information barrier against tautological specifications; beyond Dafny and JML I found no fetched work that mutates ACSL or SPARK contracts, so the Frama-C and SPARK legs look open, with Verus and Coq leads still to check.

key_works.title: MutDafny: A Mutation-Based Approach to Assess Dafny Specifications
key_works.what: Mutates the program with 40 operators (some from existing tools, some mined from Dafny bugfix commits), uses the specs as the detector, and reports five weak real-world specs (about one per 241 lines) over 794 Dafny programs. The fetched abstract reports no overall kill or survival rate and only a subset of surviving mutants analysed by hand. Closest analogue to a twin-based adequacy check, but it mutates code, not specs.

key_works.title: IronSpec: Increasing the Reliability of Formal Specifications
key_works.what: Three parts: automated sanity checks, a Spec-Testing Proof methodology, and automated spec mutation testing. Evaluated on 14 specs (six from real verified codebases) and found ten spec bugs across all six systems. The fetched abstract does not describe the mutation or vacuity mechanics; those came only from search summaries.

key_works.title: Spec-Harness: Assessing and Guiding LLM-Synthesized Formal Specifications Beyond Verifiability
key_works.what: JML specs from LLMs, graded on pre- and postcondition correctness and completeness using Hoare-triple checks plus input/output mutation over built test suites. Headlines: 22.7% of verifier-approved specs have no postcondition; trivial postconditions such as 'ensures true' pass any verifier; verifier-feedback prompt optimisation does not beat the best hand-written prompt. No venue stated (v1 31 Mar 2026, v3 9 Oct 2026).

key_works.what: Introduces correctness and discriminative-power metrics for LLM-generated postconditions. The fetched abstract reports that the generated postconditions caught 64 real historical bugs from Defects4J. Its mutant-based completeness details come only from search summaries.

key_works.title: Beyond Postconditions: Can Large Language Models infer Formal Contracts for Automatic Software Verification?
key_works.what: NL2Contract: LLMs produce pre- and postconditions evaluated on soundness, bug discriminative power and usability in automatic verification. The fetched abstract says contracts are generally sound for all inputs, separate buggy from correct code, and cut verifier false alarms versus postconditions alone. The abstract gives no numbers; the accept@1 and sound@1 figures in search summaries are unconfirmed.

key_works.title: Containment Verification: AI Safety Guarantees Independent of Alignment
key_works.what: The fetched abstract says the agentic pipeline generates the spec, model and proof under an information barrier against tautological specifications. Its section 4.4 vacuity gate (a stripped proof stub must be rejected) and discrimination gate (a seeded modelling error must be caught), adapted from IronSpec-style mutation checks, come from a search summary; section 4.4 was not reached by fetch. Closest in pattern to dawnr's twin gate, but framed as AI safety.

findings.relation_to_dawnr:
Overlap is high, and part of the twin idea is not original. Using a deliberately wrong variant to test a spec is prior art: IronSpec (OSDI 2024) and MutDafny (ICSE 2026) for Dafny, Spec-Harness (2026) for JML, and Containment Verification (2026) for LLM-written Dafny specs. The twin itself also appears in SWE-Proof (arXiv 2609.21190, search-level: a pre-fix twin that must fail to verify), and dawnr's own 10/7 survey already says 'The twin itself is no longer unique' (/home/t/Projects/t-proof-engine/internal/RESEARCH-2026-10-07-landscape-survey.md line 56). What remains distinctive is the certificate form: a kill is a kernel-accepted refutation at a stated concrete input (/home/t/Projects/t-proof-engine/ENGINE.md lines 21-24), required in all seven kernels. I did not find a fetched work that runs one mutation check across several verifiers: MutDafny and IronSpec are Dafny-only, Spec-Harness is JML-only, and nl2postcond checks against tests. The motivating premise is confirmed: Spec-Harness's 22.7% figure and its 'ensures true' example show that verifier acceptance is not evidence of adequacy.

Three cautions. First, dawnr's 100% twin-refutation share (/home/t/Projects/t-proof-engine/internal/RESEARCH-2026-10-06-landscape.md rows at lines 41-42, planned as headline metric D3 at line 82) is measured over a fixed set of task-chosen twins and witnesses (426 real/twin pairs over 213 verified programs, ENGINE.md line 190). It shows the gate discriminates on chosen edits, not how many wrong programs a spec rejects. Second, ENGINE.md uses 'vacuous' to mean 'cannot tell the twin apart', while the literature (IronSpec, Containment, and the temporal model-checking vacuity notion Containment cites as Beer et al., 2001) uses it for trivially satisfied specs such as empty proofs or unreachable antecedents. The two overlap but are not the same, and dawnr should say which it means. Third, the gate checks discrimination, not intent: a misformalized spec can refute every chosen twin. Search-level work on intent formalization (arXiv 2406.09757) reports mutation-based scoring marking a benchmark-labelled strong spec incomplete (0.6), so the gate should be described as discrimination, not faithfulness.
opportunities: Cross-verifier mutation adequacy: none of the works I fetched runs one spec-mutation check across several verifiers. A seven-kernel kill matrix in which each kill is a kernel-accepted witness would be the first such dataset in my searches.

Unfiltered kill rates per operator and per kernel: report kills over the full operator set before the gate filters, and list survivors. MutDafny's abstract reports no overall kill rate, and dawnr's current 100% refutation share is over chosen twins, so a published matrix would be the stronger artifact.

Survivor triage with witnesses: MutDafny hand-analysed only a subset of surviving mutants. A bounded witness search per survivor, checked by the kernels, either kills it (evidence of a weak spec) or leaves an equivalence question. Kills need no equivalence judgement; survivors do, and LLM-based equivalent-mutant detection is itself an open problem (Tian et al., ISSTA 2024, search-level).

Disagreements as differential findings: all seven kernels must agree, so every disagreement is currently just a refusal. Logging each one as a bug candidate for a kernel or lowering is differential testing of the toolchain. Search-level evidence of yield: Dafny compiler fuzzing (ICST 2024) reports 24 compiler bugs, nine of them soundness issues. ENGINE.md line 18 records a CVC5 model-converter crash on the Dafny twin path. I found no cross-verifier version of this.

Stub-based vacuity per kernel: Containment's gate (an empty or stripped proof must be rejected) and IronSpec's mutation-induced vacuity test a different failure, a spec that verifies with a trivial proof. ENGINE.md describes no-assume and no-sorry rules (the 10/7 survey, line 79, mentions them) that cover part of this; a per-kernel empty-stub rejection check is not described and looks cheap to add.

Open legs: Frama-C ACSL and SPARK contract mutation returned nothing in my searches, so those legs look open, and Rocq has a 2019 Coq mutation-analysis precedent (Celik et al., search-level). Do not claim Verus is open yet: search results point to a verus-lang/verus-spec-check repo with spec mutation features and to cargo-verus-mutants, neither fetched. Verus-SpecGym (arXiv 2605.26457, search-level) reports LLM judges missed 25.7% of wrong specs that executable tests flagged, which supports test-grounded checks.

Comparable public-benchmark audit: MutDafny's five weak specs in 794 programs (about one per 241 lines) give a published yardstick for dawnr's planned D8 twin audit of public verified benchmarks (/home/t/Projects/t-proof-engine/NORTH-STAR.md line 19). Running the same count on a shared corpus would allow a direct comparison.

Not searched: metamorphic relations on specs (for example permutation or scaling invariance on sequence and float specs) and model-counting measures of spec strength (how many outputs a spec admits over a bounded domain). Check both before claiming novelty.
findings.direction_hint: Turn the binary twin gate into a measured kill matrix before adding more gates. Take the 426 real/twin pairs in t/twins/, whose twins carry an operator and witness (ENGINE.md line 170); add MutDafny-style operators mined from bugfix commits in each kernel's public projects; refute every mutant in all seven kernels with its witness; and publish kill rates per operator and per kernel with a hand-triaged survivor list. Report survivors rather than requiring 100% kill, since sound survivors exist and strict targets penalise them (SWE-Proof, search-level).

findings.dimension: Small and data-efficient language models: data quality over scale (phi and textbook-quality data, distillation, curation, more-per-parameter claims and their critiques)
findings.landscape: Since phi-1 (Microsoft, 2023: 1.3B parameters trained on 6B filtered 'textbook quality' tokens plus 1B GPT-3.5 synthetic textbook and exercise tokens, 50.6% HumanEval), data quality over scale has become standard practice: Phi-4 (14B, Dec 2024) uses synthetic data throughout training, and SmolLM2 (1.7B on about 11T tokens, Feb 2025) adds newly built FineMath, Stack-Edu and SmolTalk sets to its web mix. Model-based filtering is 'key' to high-quality pretraining sets (DCLM, 2024), and distillation or small curated reasoning sets are a leading 2025 route to more per parameter (Phi-4-mini-reasoning at 3.8B beats DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B by 3.2 points on MATH-500; s1 fine-tunes a 32B base on 1,000 curated questions; LIMO reports 63.3% AIME24 from a small curated set). The critiques are now quantitative: repeated data is near-fresh only up to about 4 epochs (Muennighoff et al., NeurIPS 2023), the best filter depends on compute budget (Goyal et al., CVPR 2024), models of 3B or fewer do not reliably gain from long or strong-teacher reasoning (Small Model Learnability Gap, 2025), synthetic-only recursive training collapses unless real data is accumulated alongside (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024), and benchmark leakage can manufacture scores (Schaeffer, 2023; phi-4's decontamination is self-reported). The closest prior art to dawnr's verified-data gate is ATLAS (arXiv Dec 2025, v2 Feb 2026), which turns 2.7K machine-checked Dafny programs into 19K training examples and lifts a fine-tuned 7B Qwen coder on DafnyBench from 32.4% to 56.9%, but with one prover and existing models. Primary 2026 coverage is thin: no Phi-5 report surfaced, ATLAS v2 (revised Feb 2026) is the main 2026-dated primary paper I confirmed, and the search budget ran out before the last query.

key_works.title: Textbooks Are All You Need (phi-1)
key_works.what: 1.3B model trained on 6B filtered 'textbook quality' tokens plus 1B GPT-3.5 synthetic textbook and exercise tokens; 50.6% HumanEval pass@1, and phi-1-small (350M) reaches 45%. Origin of the data-over-scale claim; the Phi reports do not release their synthetic datasets (per the Cosmopedia post).

key_works.title: Phi-4 Technical Report
key_works.what: 14B model whose recipe is 'centrally focused on data quality' and 'strategically incorporates synthetic data throughout the training process'; claims it substantially surpasses its GPT-4 teacher on STEM QA and goes beyond distillation. The abstract gives no synthetic-token share, no phi-4 teacher name, and no decontamination details.

key_works.title: Phi-4-Mini-Reasoning: Exploring the Limits of Small Reasoning Language Models in Math
key_works.what: 3.8B model trained by mid-training on distilled long-CoT synthetic data, then SFT; beats DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B by 3.2 points and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B by 7.7 points on MATH-500. Teacher and data volume are not named in the abstract.

key_works.title: SmolLM2: When Smol Goes Big, Data-Centric Training of a Small Language Model
key_works.what: 1.7B model overtrained on about 11T tokens in multiple stages; adds newly built FineMath, Stack-Edu and SmolTalk where existing sets were problematically small or low-quality; claims to outperform Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.2-1B; model and datasets released.

key_works.title: DataComp for Language Models (DCLM)
key_works.what: Curation testbed at 412M to 7B scale where model-based filtering is key to a high-quality training set; the 7B DCLM-Baseline on 2.6T tokens reaches 64% 5-shot MMLU with 6.6x less compute than Llama 3 8B.

key_works.title: FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu
key_works.what: 15T-token FineWeb from 96 Common Crawl snapshots and a 1.3T-token educational subset; FineWeb-Edu-pretrained models perform dramatically better on MMLU and ARC. The labeler for the classifier is not named on the fetched page.

key_works.title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
key_works.what: Up to 4 epochs of repeated data gives negligible loss change versus unique data; beyond that the value of added compute decays to zero; proposes a compute-optimal law that discounts repeated tokens and excess parameters; 400 training runs released.

key_works.title: Scaling Laws for Data Filtering: Data Curation cannot be Compute Agnostic
key_works.what: The best filter depends on training compute: high-quality data loses value when repeated, so larger budgets need lower-quality data; curation cannot be agnostic of the total compute.

key_works.title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
key_works.what: s1K: 1,000 questions with reasoning traces chosen for difficulty, diversity and quality, used to SFT Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; s1-32B exceeds o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24; budget forcing lifts AIME24 from 50% to 57%.

key_works.title: LIMO: Less Is More for Reasoning
key_works.what: Hypothesis that elicitation depends on complete pretrained knowledge plus a few cognitive-template examples; reports 63.3% AIME24 and 95.6% MATH500 from only a few examples (the count of 817 comes from secondary coverage, not the abstract).

key_works.title: Small Models Struggle to Learn from Strong Reasoners
key_works.year: 2025 (Findings of ACL 2025 per the ACL Anthology listing)
key_works.what: Names the Small Model Learnability Gap: models of 3B or fewer do not consistently benefit from long chain-of-thought data or from distillation from larger teachers, and do better on shorter, simpler chains; proposes Mix Distillation, which beats either source alone (no numbers in the abstract).

key_works.title: Distilling Step-by-Step!
key_works.what: A 770M T5 student trained with LLM rationales as extra supervision beats few-shot prompted 540B PaLM on one benchmark while using 80% of the data; standard finetuning of the same student does not match even with all the data.

key_works.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
key_works.what: Abstract says the reasoning patterns of larger models can be systematically harnessed to guide and enhance smaller models; the distilled-model sizes and comparisons were not on the fetched page.

key_works.title: Cosmopedia: how to create large-scale synthetic data for pre-training
key_works.what: Open replication of the phi-1.5 synthetic-textbook recipe: 30M files and 25B tokens generated by Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct from web-clustered topics, audiences and styles; pipeline, dataset and cosmo-1b released; cosmo-1b trails Phi-1.5 on some benchmarks.

key_works.title: ATLAS: Automated Toolkit for Large-Scale Verified Code Synthesis
key_works.who: Baksys, Zetzsche, Bouissou, Delmas, Kong, Holden
key_works.what: From TACO Python problems, 2.7K Dafny programs with machine-checked proofs, expanded to 19K training examples; fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 7B Coder goes from 32.4% to 56.9% on DafnyBench and 15.8% to 65.8% on DafnySynthesis. Closest prior art to verifier-filtered training data, but one prover, an existing 7B model, and the abstract does not detail the training filter.

key_works.title: Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data
key_works.what: Training each generation only on the previous generation's synthetic output tends toward collapse; accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data keeps test error bounded regardless of iteration count (linear-model theory plus experiments).

key_works.title: Pretraining on the Test Set Is All You Need
key_works.what: A satirical 1M-parameter model (phi-CTNL) trained on under 100k tokens built only from evaluation benchmarks, reporting perfect results; the arXiv comment field labels it satire. A warning that small-model benchmark scores can be manufactured.

key_works.title: TinyStories: How Small Can Language Models Be and Still Speak Coherent English?
key_works.what: Models under 10M parameters write fluent multi-paragraph stories after training on GPT-3.5/GPT-4-generated simple-vocabulary stories; GPT-4 used as a multidimensional grader. Narrow-domain precedent for synthetic data in a tiny model.

key_works.title: Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI
key_works.what: Position paper arguing SLMs are sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable and necessarily more economical for repetitive agent invocations, and inviting critique; it names barriers only in general terms and offers no measured evidence in the abstract.

key_works.title: Sensitivity of Small Language Models to Fine-tuning Data Contamination
key_works.what: 23 SLMs from 270M to 4B parameters: character-reversal contamination of fine-tuning data causes near-complete failure across all models; semantic contamination is more tolerable; larger models learn semantic corruption more readily (a capability curse).

key_works.title: Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning
key_works.what: Theory that a high-quality pruning metric can beat power-law scaling in dataset size, shown on ResNets for CIFAR-10, SVHN and ImageNet; the easy-versus-hard pruning rule was not on the fetched page.

key_works.title: MobileLLM-R1: Exploring the Limits of Sub-Billion Language Model Reasoners with Open Training Recipes
key_works.what: Claims a 950M reasoning model reaches parity with or exceeds Qwen3-0.6B on several reasoning evals using about 4.2T resampled tokens from a roughly 2T curated pool, versus Qwen3's 36T. Secondary coverage is garbled and shows Qwen3-0.6B ahead on GSM8K; one write-up flags a non-commercial licence (not checked here).

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap and prior art: the general claim that curated or teacher-generated data lets a small model beat its size class is already published (phi-1, Phi-4, Cosmopedia, SmolLM2, TinyStories), so dawnr cannot present curated synthetic data helping small models as new; its distinct question, whether verified data beats raw code per parameter, is the same question these papers answer with classifiers or rubrics. Confirmation: curation is a measured lever (DCLM, FineWeb-Edu), checked reasoning traces work at small scale (s1, LIMO, Phi-4-mini-reasoning), and verifier-filtered synthetic data already moves a 7B model on Dafny (ATLAS, 32.4% to 56.9% on DafnyBench). Threat to the verifier gate as a novelty claim: ATLAS already shows that verified formal data trains better models, but with one prover and existing 7B models, so dawnr's defensible novelty is the seven-kernel conjunction, the one-edit twin refutation as an adequacy filter, and from-scratch per-parameter measurement; none of those three appeared in this search, which was not exhaustive. Pressures the literature puts on the roughly 93M from-scratch locallm student: the Small Model Learnability Gap argues for short, simple targets or a mix rather than long traces or strong-teacher copies; repeated-data results make unique verified rows, not parameters, the binding limit, which matches the project's own data is the limit finding; Goyal et al. imply the verifier's strictness should be tuned to the compute budget rather than fixed at maximum; Scaria et al. show that character-reversal contamination nearly eliminates capability in 270M to 4B models, which supports keeping the syntax check hard. Per-parameter claims are gameable (Schaeffer, 2023; phi-4's decontamination is self-reported), so dawnr's held-out panels and heldout audit are an asset the cited small-model reports lack. Teacher choice is constrained by the project's standing rules (Apache or MIT teachers only for training rows, no OpenAI outputs in training rows), which most distillation recipes above do not face. The Belcak et al. position supports the offline small-model CLI direction, but it is an argument, not evidence.
opportunities: Multi-prover admission as a training filter: no primary paper found that trains a small model on rows admitted by several independent kernels and reports gain per verified token; ATLAS uses one prover and fine-tunes a 7B model.

One-edit twin refutation as a data-adequacy filter: the work found here checks correctness (ATLAS uses test cases) but not whether the specification is strong enough to reject a broken twin; a reproducible mutation gate is a citable contribution.

Matched-budget curves: publish gain against unique verified tokens at equal parameter count for raw code versus verified rows, on the Goyal and Muennighoff axes; none of the small-model reports above publishes this for a formal language.

Contamination-audited per-parameter reporting: phi-4's decontamination is self-reported and Schaeffer (2023) shows the failure mode; a published held-out audit protocol is a reference most small-model papers lack.

Graded admission thresholds for formal data, tested against the Goyal et al. prediction that the best filter depends on compute; how strict a verifier should be at each token budget is open for formal languages.
Corruption tolerance for a formal language: Scaria et al. measured corruption of natural-language instruction data; corruption of t syntax and proof text is unmeasured in the literature found here.

Product angle: an offline CLI whose tools are formal checkers is a concrete test of the Belcak et al. SLM-for-agents position; a measured hallucination reduction would be evidence that the position paper lacks.
findings.direction_hint: Make the matched-budget verified-data curve the next experiment. Start from a pretrained, permissively licensed base of 0.5 to 1.5B parameters (the ladder plan's Apache-2.0 choice, with the licence checked on the model card) and train three arms at equal unique-token counts: raw t code, t rows admitted by the full seven-kernel plus twin gate, and the same gated rows at a looser admission threshold. Use short, simple targets (Small Model Learnability Gap), cap repetition near 4 epochs (Muennighoff et al.), accumulate the corpus rather than replacing it (Gerstgrasser et al.), and report gain per verified token and per parameter on the contamination-audited held-out panel. That produces the curve the literature has not published for a formal language and shows whether the gate's extra cost buys more per parameter.

findings.dimension: Benchmarks and datasets of verified code and specifications (DafnyBench, Clover, Vericoding, AlgoVeri, VERINA, CLEVER, FVAPPS, VerifyThisBench, AutoVerus) and contamination in code and proof benchmarks
findings.landscape: Verified-code benchmarks have moved from small hand-built single-language sets (Clover's hand-designed Dafny programs in 2023, then DafnyBench's over 750 Dafny programs in 2024) to large and cross-language suites in 2025-2026: Vericoding has 12,504 specifications across Dafny, Verus and Lean, and AlgoVeri (accepted to ICML 2026) enforces identical functional contracts for 77 classical algorithms in those three languages. Headline numbers depend heavily on the suite: Vericoding reports roughly 82% Dafny, 44% Verus and 27% Lean for off-the-shelf models, while AlgoVeri's frontier scores are 40.3%, 24.7% and 7.8%, and end-to-end Lean suites are harder still (VERINA's current abstract gives o3 72.6% correct code, 52.3% sound-and-complete specs and 4.9% proofs). Spec adequacy is now an explicit design target: CLEVER requires a spec equivalent to a held-out reference and excludes leaky or vacuous specs, and Clover reports up to 87% acceptance of correct programs with no false positives on adversarial wrong ones, while FVAPPS derives its Lean theorems directly from APPS unit tests, so its strength is capped by test coverage. Agentic verifier-feedback loops now handle most of a 150-task Verus suite (AutoVerus, OOPSLA 2025, reports over 90% valid proofs), so the headline depends on the suite as much as on the method. None of the nine benchmark abstracts I fetched reports a contamination analysis.

key_works.title: DafnyBench: A Benchmark for Formal Software Verification
key_works.year: 2024 (arXiv June 2024; a Dafny 2025 workshop listing at POPL appeared in search)
key_works.what: Over 750 Dafny programs (about 53k lines); the model must write verifier hints until each program verifies; best model and prompt reach 68%, retry with verifier feedback helps, and success falls as code and hint count grow. Dawnr relevance: the standard Dafny-only hint-writing baseline; the abstract does not describe sourcing or contamination.

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation (CloverBench)
key_works.who: Chuyue Sun, Ying Sheng, Oded Padon, Clark Barrett
key_works.year: 2023 (arXiv Oct 2023, v4 Nov 2024; a SAIV 2024 version appeared in search)
key_works.what: Checks consistency between code, docstrings and Dafny annotations using a verifier plus an LLM; accepts up to 87% of correct programs with no false positives on adversarial incorrect ones; flags 6 wrong programs in MBPP-DFY-50. Dawnr relevance: the closest published ancestor of the twin idea, though its abstract describes no systematic one-edit twin construction.

key_works.title: VERINA: Benchmarking Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.who: Ye et al. (sunblaze-ucb group, per search)
key_works.what: 189 manually curated Lean tasks, each with a description, reference code, formal spec and tests; separate code, spec (soundness and completeness) and proof metrics; the current abstract reports o3 at 72.6% code, 52.3% spec and 4.9% proof, while v1 reported o4-mini at 61.4/51.0/3.6 per search, so figures moved between versions. Dawnr relevance: proof is the bottleneck, and separate per-stage metrics are the reporting model to copy.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.who: Beneficial AI Foundation (repo owner per search; authors not on the abstract page)
key_works.year: 2025 (arXiv Sep 2025; a Dafny 2026 workshop listing at POPL appeared in search)
key_works.what: 12,504 formal specifications: 3,029 Dafny, 2,334 Verus/Rust, 7,141 Lean; 6,174 are labelled new unseen problems; off-the-shelf success about 82% Dafny, 44% Verus, 27% Lean. Dawnr relevance: the largest multi-language public suite and the most direct yardstick for a multi-kernel claim, but its abstract does not analyze overlap in the non-new items.

key_works.title: AlgoVeri: An Aligned Benchmark for Verified Code Generation on Classical Algorithms
key_works.who: Haoyu Zhao, Ziran Yang, Jiawei Li, Deyuan He, Zenan Li, Chi Jin, Venugopal V. Veeravalli, Aarti Gupta, Sanjeev Arora
key_works.year: 2026 (arXiv Feb 2026, v2 Jun 2026; accepted to ICML 2026 per its comments)
