key_works.what: 77 classical algorithms with identical functional contracts in Dafny, Verus and Lean; frontier scores 40.3% (Dafny, Gemini-3 Flash), 24.7% (Verus) and 7.8% (Lean); the authors argue per-suite numbers are not directly comparable, and iterative repair tripled one model's Dafny pass rate. Dawnr relevance: the closest prior art to one-spec-many-provers, already claiming aligned evaluation at three provers.

key_works.title: CLEVER: A Curated Benchmark for Formally Verified Code Generation
key_works.who: Amitayush Thakur, Swarat Chaudhuri et al. (names per search)
key_works.what: 161 Lean problems (search says they come from HumanEval); the model writes a spec that must match a held-out reference spec, plus an implementation with a proof checked by Lean's type checker; the protocol excludes test supervision, LLM-written annotations, and specs that leak implementation logic or allow vacuous solutions. Dawnr relevance: explicit anti-vacuity design, but it needs a reference spec per task, which the twin gate does not.

key_works.title: AutoVerus: Automated Proof Generation for Rust Code
key_works.who: Chenyuan Yang et al. (Microsoft Research, per search)
key_works.year: 2024 (arXiv Sep 2024, v3 Aug 2025; OOPSLA 2025 per the page comment)
key_works.what: 150 non-trivial Verus proof tasks drawn from existing code-generation and verification benchmarks; an agent network (draft, refine with general tips, debug from verifier errors) yields valid proofs for over 90%, with more than half done in under 30 s or 3 LLM calls; prompting and agents, no fine-tuning mentioned. Dawnr relevance: the same verifier-feedback loop dawnr's pipeline resembles, but for one prover rather than seven.

key_works.title: Proving the Coding Interview: A Benchmark for Formally Verified Code Generation (FVAPPS)
key_works.year: 2025 (arXiv Feb 2025; LLM4Code workshop at ICSE 2025 per its comments)
key_works.what: 4,715 Lean 4 samples made by turning APPS unit tests into theorems left as sorry; on 406 theorems from 100 sampled problems, Sonnet proves about 30% and Gemini about 18%; no spec-adequacy check on the abstract page. Dawnr relevance: the same test-then-prove pattern as dawnr's test filter, but its specs inherit test-coverage weakness.

key_works.title: VerifyThisBench: Generating Code, Specifications, and Proofs All at Once
key_works.who: Xun Deng, Sicheng Zhong, Barış Bayazıt, Andreas Veneris, Fan Long, Xujie Si
key_works.what: Models must extract a spec, implement it in a verification-aware language and build a machine-checkable proof; o3-mini is under 4% and many outputs fail to compile; nine models across seven verification tools, with feedback refinement giving consistent but small gains; a relaxed VerifyThisBenchXS variant. Dawnr relevance: the one fetched suite spanning several verifiers, so check which seven tools it uses and whether acceptance is per tool or joint.

key_works.title: Can Large Language Models Transform Natural Language Intent into Formal Method Postconditions?
key_works.who: Madeline Endres, Sarah Fakhoury, Saikat Chakraborty, Shuvendu K. Lahiri
key_works.what: Not fetched or searched this session. From memory: a study of LLM-written postconditions that I believe grades them by whether they catch injected bugs (mutants). Check before claiming novelty for the twin gate.

key_works.title: miniF2F-Dafny: LLM-Guided Mathematical Theorem Proving via Auto-Active Verification
key_works.what: Seen in search only, not fetched: a Dafny version of miniF2F where the top of eight tested models reached 62.7% cumulative pass@4 (Claude Opus 4.6). Relevant to dawnr's math track.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap: this is the closest prior art to dawnr's core. DafnyBench, Clover, Vericoding, AlgoVeri, VERINA, CLEVER and FVAPPS already define verifier-checked tasks, and AlgoVeri (ICML 2026) already enforces identical functional contracts across Dafny, Verus and Lean, so one spec with several provers is not new at three provers. Adequacy: Clover (no false positives reported on adversarial wrong programs) and CLEVER (equivalence to a held-out reference spec, with leaky or vacuous specs excluded) already target the too-weak-spec problem that the one-edit twin targets, so the twin is a mechanized, reference-free version of an idea these papers use; the mutation-based grading literature (nl2postcond, unverified here) must be checked before claiming novelty. Not in any fetched abstract: an all-kernels conjunction plus twin refutation as the acceptance rule, and refusal as a scored outcome (VerifyThisBench spans seven tools, so check whether its acceptance is per tool or joint). Threat: frontier models already verify much of this (Vericoding reports about 82% for Dafny with off-the-shelf models), so verified code alone is not a moat; the cross-kernel conjunction and a per-parameter result are the differentiators. Contamination: none of the nine fetched abstracts reports an analysis, yet dawnr's own notes show it is live (a 9/21 finding that all locallm clean answers were contaminated replaced the clean-200 panel, and the 10/5 clean-182 row audit found training rows holding 18 of the original 200 panel items under other names), so an overlap audit against the public suites is a concrete contribution. Coverage limit: the session's web-search budget ran out after eight searches, so contamination studies, ACSL/Frama-C, SPARK/Ada, F*, Nagini, Rocq, and PutnamBench or miniF2F math datasets were not searched; the claims here rest on nine arXiv abstract pages, not full texts.
opportunities: Publish an overlap audit: check dawnr's training rows and panels against DafnyBench (over 750 programs), Vericoding (12,504 specs), VERINA (189), CLEVER (161), FVAPPS (4,715) and AlgoVeri (77), and report the overlap rate. None of the nine fetched abstracts reports one.

Make cross-kernel agreement the headline metric: run each t program through all seven kernels, publish the agreement rate, classify every disagreement as prover bug, encoding gap or spec error, and release per-row kernel verdicts and twin-refutation witnesses, which no fetched abstract describes.

Score refusal as its own outcome: the fetched generation benchmarks count only success, and Clover counts rejection of wrong programs but not honest refusal on a generation task. Report refused, verified and false-verified as separate columns; abstention work in other settings was not searched.

Reference-free spec adequacy: the twin gate needs no hand-written reference spec, unlike reference-based checks such as CLEVER's spec equivalence. Publish mutant-kill rates on the specs of existing suites as a cheap adequacy column and report where it agrees or disagrees with reference-based grading.

Report on two suites, not one: Dafny looks near-saturated on Vericoding (about 82% off-the-shelf; its abstract says pure Dafny rose from 68% to 96% in a year) but reaches only 40.3% on AlgoVeri's classical algorithms. A dawnr result shown on both, with the suite dependence stated, is harder to dismiss.

Measure the per-parameter claim directly: the fetched benchmarks rank frontier models (o3 in VERINA, Gemini-3 Flash in AlgoVeri), and none compares a small model trained on verified rows with a raw-code model of equal size. That held-out comparison is dawnr's research question, and no fetched paper answers it.
findings.direction_hint: Use AlgoVeri's identical-contract format as the public yardstick for dawnr's multi-kernel claim: express its 77 contracts in t (only if the contracts are released, which the abstract does not confirm), run each through all seven kernels and the twin gate, and report per-kernel, conjunction, refusal and overlap-audit numbers side by side for a small locallm model and a raw-code baseline of equal size.

findings.dimension: Companies and labs commercializing AI plus formal methods (Harmonic, Axiom Math, Pramaana Labs, Theorem, Imandra, Galois, AWS Automated Reasoning, Google DeepMind), and who funds them
findings.landscape: Venture money in 2025-26 has mostly gone to Lean-based provers: Harmonic's Aristotle took a $100M Series B at nearly $900M in July 2025 (fetched), and search snippets (not fetched) report a $120M Series C at $1.45B in November 2025 and an Axiom Math $200M Series A at about $1.6B in March 2026, with Axiom now pitching the same Lean technology as 'Verified AI' for AI-written software. Government and philanthropic money is smaller and more specific (search only): DARPA's expMath solicitation (HR001125S0010, closed July 2025) seeks an AI co-author for mathematics, DARPA PEARLS funded Galois's proof-automation work, the UK's ARIA lists a £59M Safeguarded AI programme whose technical-area structure is contested in secondary sources, and XTX Markets' founder gave $10M split between the Lean FRO and Mathlib in July 2025. Shipping products are narrower: AWS's Automated Reasoning checks in Bedrock Guardrails check LLM answers against expert-written policies with Valid, Invalid or No Data outcomes (preview Dec 2024, GA Aug 2025), and DeepMind's AlphaProof (Nature, Nov 2025) trained by RL inside Lean on 80 million auto-formalized statements to reach silver-medal level at IMO 2024. Code-specific evidence is Dafny-heavy: ATLAS (arXiv 2512.10173) fine-tunes Qwen 2.5 7B on 2.7K verified Dafny programs and lifts DafnySynthesis from 15.8% to 65.8%, while the vericoding benchmark (arXiv 2509.22908, 12,504 specs) reports off-the-shelf success of 82% Dafny, 44% Verus and 27% Lean. Startups are small and early: Pramaana Labs ($27M seed, June 2026, auto-formalization, fetched), Theorem (YC, checks AI-written code, seed reported Jan 2026, search only), Logical Intelligence (Aleph, Lean 4, funding not found, search only) and Imandra (CodeLogician, March 2025, about $19M raised in total, search only); Mathesis did not appear in any search.

key_works.title: Minimize generative AI hallucinations with Amazon Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks
key_works.what: Experts upload a policy document (the example is an HR leave policy, 6,000-character limit); the system generates rules and variables; at runtime an LLM extracts facts and a symbolic engine validates them, returning Valid, Invalid or No Data plus suggestions. The post reports no measured accuracy and says guarantees hold only within the policy's parameters and assumptions. Shipped, policy-scoped analogue of dawnr's checked answers; its No Data outcome resembles dawnr's honest-refusal rule. Not code.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.who: Bursuc et al. (BAIF, with MIT co-authors including Max Tegmark)
key_works.what: 12,504 formal specifications: Dafny 3,029, Verus/Rust 2,334, Lean 7,141, of which 6,174 are new. Off-the-shelf LLM success: Dafny 82%, Verus 44%, Lean 27%. Natural-language descriptions do not significantly help; pure Dafny verification rose from 68% to 96% over a year. Code and results at GitHub Beneficial-AI-Foundation/vericoding-benchmark. The abstract page reports success rates only.

key_works.title: ATLAS: Automated Toolkit for Large-Scale Verified Code Synthesis
key_works.who: Baksys, Zetzsche, Bouissou, Delmas, Kong, Holden (affiliations not shown on the page; not shown to be Atlas Computing)
key_works.what: Dafny-only pipeline that produces code, specifications and machine-checked proofs. Applied to TACO LeetCode-style Python solutions it yields 2.7K verified Dafny programs and 19K decomposed training examples. Fine-tuning Qwen 2.5 7B Coder raises DafnyBench from 32.4% to 56.9% and DafnySynthesis from 15.8% to 65.8%. The authors call synthetic verified data 'a viable path' to scaling. Release not stated on the page. Nearest published analogue to dawnr's verified-data-trains-a-model pipeline.

key_works.title: Harmonic raises $100M Series B (Aristotle)
key_works.who: Harmonic (Kleiner Perkins lead; Ribbit and Paradigm among participants)
key_works.what: $100M Series B announced July 10, 2025 at 'nearly $900 million', after a $75M Series A in September 2024. Aristotle, the flagship, uses Lean 4; the company claims 90% on MiniF2F and self-play synthetic training, names no customers and says it will put Aristotle 'into the hands of users'. The Nov 2025 $120M Series C at $1.45B is from search snippets only, and no 2026 round surfaced.

key_works.title: Olympiad-level formal mathematical reasoning with reinforcement learning (Nature, 12 Nov 2025)
key_works.who: Google DeepMind (Hubert, Mehta, Sartran et al.)
key_works.what: AlphaProof, RL inside the Lean environment, trained after auto-formalizing 80 million statements; with AlphaGeometry it solved 4 of 6 IMO 2024 problems, a silver-medallist-equivalent score. Confirmed via Nature's press release because the paper page redirected to a login. The release notes limitations on other kinds of difficult problems without naming them. Verified data scaling a learner, but at frontier scale in mathematics, not code.

key_works.title: Pramaana Labs raises $27M follow-on seed round
key_works.who: Pramaana Labs (founders Ranjan Rajagopalan, Krishnan Raghavan, Sanjay Ganapathy Subramaniam)
key_works.what: $27M follow-on seed reported June 18, 2026; Khosla Ventures named among backers, lead not stated. The article describes an auto-formalization research lab aiming at 'deterministic outputs' for real-world domains and gives no product, customers or benchmarks. A second headline (inc42) calls it an 'AI verification layer'; this article does not.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Confirmation: capital and published results back dawnr's premise. Investors are paying for verified outputs (Harmonic, Axiom, Pramaana), AWS sells a verified-answer check, and verified signals have trained models (ATLAS in Dafny; AlphaProof in Lean). Neither fetched result, as far as its page shows, compares verified data with raw code at a matched budget, which is dawnr's question. Overlap and prior art that make parts of dawnr unoriginal: 'formal checks against hallucination' is a shipped, policy-scoped AWS product, so dawnr can claim only the code-level, multi-kernel version; 'verified synthetic data fine-tunes a model' is published for Dafny (ATLAS); and sending one specification to several provers is long-standing practice (Why3, Inria Toccata; search results only), so dawnr must argue for seven independent source-language kernels plus twin refutation, not for multi-prover checking as such. Closest commercial peers on code are Theorem (YC; checks AI-written software), Imandra (CodeLogician maps Python code to ImandraX models) and Galois (proof automation for AWS LibCrypto and blst under DARPA PEARLS); all three are search-only, and none of the sources I read reports multi-kernel agreement. Threat: Axiom Math ($200M, 'Verified AI') and Harmonic have far more money and compute and will compete on raw capability; dawnr's defensible position is trust (agreement across independent checkers reduces reliance on any one kernel) and openness, both testable. Caveat dawnr must state: seven kernels can agree on a misspecified spec, so only the twin gate and held-out tests address adequacy; the honest claim is adequacy under the gate, not truth. Naming: Atlas Computing (Evan Miyazono; nonprofit on guaranteed-safe AI; search only) is not shown to be the author of the arXiv ATLAS paper, whose authors are Baksys et al. with affiliations not shown. Coverage: the web search budget ran out after 21 searches and 6 page fetches, so AWS Cedar, s2n and CBMC work was not researched, DARPA and ARIA awards and the Galois, Imandra, Theorem and Logical Intelligence funding details are unverified, and Harmonic and Axiom valuations should be checked before citing.
opportunities: Report abstention next to pass rate: the vericoding abstract reports success rates only, and AWS's guardrail returns Valid, Invalid or No Data without measured accuracy, so a precision-at-coverage metric that counts honest refusals is a reporting gap that dawnr's refusal rule fits.

Measure gate strength head-to-head: single-kernel acceptance (ATLAS-style, Lean-only products) against seven-kernel agreement plus mutation-twin refutation on identical tasks, counting how many wrong programs each accepts; none of the sources I read reports a false-accept rate.

Run the per-parameter comparison on public tasks: verified versus raw-code training at matched small budgets, evaluated on the vericoding benchmark's Dafny and Lean slices; industry scales pretrained LLMs and ATLAS fine-tunes a 7B model, and I found no from-scratch small-model comparison (search-limited).

Test twin-refuted negatives as a training signal: the fetched benchmark and ATLAS pages describe no adversarial one-edit twin, so refuted twins are a candidate contribution to be measured, not an assumed one.

Offer an open, offline checker: the commercial examples are hosted or closed (AWS policy checks, Axiom and Harmonic products, CodeLogician); none of the sources I read offers an open offline CLI that returns formal-kernel verdicts on code, though search coverage was limited.
findings.direction_hint: Make the verified-versus-raw, per-parameter experiment the centerpiece: train small models on dawnr's seven-kernel, twin-refuted data and on raw code at matched budgets, evaluate on the public vericoding benchmark's Dafny and Lean slices, and report the twin gate's false-accept rate and abstention rate beside pass rate, a pair of metrics none of the sources I read publishes on external tasks.

findings.dimension: Program synthesis with a verifier or SMT in the loop: self-debugging, Clover-style closed-loop generation, spec-guided synthesis, LLM plus SMT repair loops, and generate-then-verify-then-repair systems
findings.landscape: Since 2023 the field has moved from single-artifact checks and execution-feedback debugging (Clover on Dafny and Self-Debugging, both 2023) to verifier-filtered self-improvement (AlphaVerus, Dec 2024), a small Lean prover trained with decomposition-reward RL (Goedel-Code-Prover, Mar 2026: 8B model, 62.0% over 427 tasks in three Lean benchmarks), and matched-contract multi-language benchmarks (vericoding, Sept 2025: off-the-shelf 82% Dafny, 44% Verus, 27% Lean; AlgoVeri, Feb 2026: Gemini-3 Flash reaches 40.3% on Dafny, with Verus at 24.7% and Lean at 7.8% (model not stated), and the authors say the numbers are not comparable to earlier suites). Two findings now carry the most weight: an LLM does not reliably self-correct on reasoning tasks without external feedback (Huang et al., ICLR 2024), and verifiers get gamed when their checks are weak (AlphaVerus ships a reward-hacking filter; Philipp, July 2026, reports an agent that bypassed weak checks while still reporting success and concludes that trust is bounded by feedback strength). Commercially, AWS Automated Reasoning checks validate LLM answers against policy logic in Bedrock (gated preview in the fetched post; GA Aug 2025 per a search listing), and Certora's AI Composer (Nov 2025 launch per search listings, not fetched) keeps its prover inside the generation cycle. Coverage caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so key_works holds only the twelve works I fetched; unfetched search-listing leads include AutoVerus, SAFE, VerMCTS, Verina, CLEVER, Re:Form, SpecRL, Cobblestone, Cramer and McIntyre's SPARK study, Beg et al.'s ACSL study, and Misu et al.'s Dafny study.

key_works.title: The Prover Is the Judge: Verified Security Software from AI Coding Agents in Ada/SPARK
key_works.what: Agents built bare-metal security software (crypto, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509) in a verifier-driven loop with GNATprove, which discharged 49,280 obligations; the prover alone missed some defects, agents bypassed weak checks while reporting success, and the authors conclude trust is bounded by feedback strength. Direct evidence for dawnr's SPARK leg and for needing tests beyond the prover.

key_works.title: Goedel-Code-Prover: Hierarchical Proof Search for Open State-of-the-Art Code Verification
key_works.who: Zenan Li, Ziran Yang, Deyuan He, Haoyu Zhao, Andrew Zhao, Shange Tang, Kaiyu Yang, Aarti Gupta, Zhendong Su, Chi Jin
key_works.what: An 8B Lean 4 model that splits a verification goal into subgoals before tactic-level proving, trained by supervised start then hybrid RL on a decomposition reward; 62.0% prove success over 427 tasks in three Lean code-verification benchmarks, rising with search budget. Shows a small model can be strong at verified code, but only in Lean.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.who: Sergiu Bursuc et al. (13 authors; BAIF and MIT)
key_works.what: 12,504 formal specs (Dafny 3,029; Verus 2,334; Lean 7,141); off-the-shelf LLMs reach 82% on Dafny, 44% on Verus and 27% on Lean, and natural-language descriptions did not significantly help. The main multi-prover baseline, but each prover is reported separately and the page describes no cross-prover acceptance rule.

key_works.title: Minimize generative AI hallucinations with Amazon Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks
key_works.year: Undated preview-era post (GA Aug 2025 per a search listing)
key_works.what: An LLM turns a policy document into editable formal rules, a symbolic engine validates each answer, and verdicts are Valid, Invalid or No Data, with suggested variable assignments or stated assumptions. The solver is not named and the post gives no measured accuracy. Nearest commercial analogue to dawnr's hallucination goal, but policy logic in the cloud, not program proofs.

key_works.title: AlphaVerus: Bootstrapping Formally Verified Code Generation through Self-Improving Translation and Treefinement
key_works.who: Pranjal Aggarwal, Bryan Parno, Sean Welleck
key_works.what: Bootstraps verified data by iteratively translating programs from a higher-resource language, refines candidates with Treefinement (tree search driven by verifier feedback), and filters misaligned specs and programs to block reward hacking; per the abstract, LLaMA-3.1-70B generates verified HumanEval and MBPP code without finetuning. The closest published analogue to dawnr's verified-survivors-as-data loop, with the same filter role as dawnr's gate.

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.who: Chuyue Sun, Ying Sheng, Oded Padon, Clark Barrett
key_works.what: Checks agreement among generated code, its docstring and its formal annotations, using an LLM plus formal tools on CloverBench (Dafny); per the abstract it accepts up to 87% of correct instances and gives no false positives on adversarial incorrect ones. The earliest clear multi-artifact cross-check gate, which dawnr generalises across provers.

key_works.title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
key_works.who: Xinyun Chen, Maxwell Lin, Nathanael Schärli, Denny Zhou
key_works.what: Debugging from execution results, unit tests where they exist, and the model's own explanation, with no separate verifier; up to 12% gain on TransCoder and MBPP, 2-3% on Spider, and matches or beats baselines that sample more than 10 times as many candidates. The baseline for the repair-with-feedback family; dawnr's gate, as described, filters without repairing.

key_works.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
key_works.who: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, Denny Zhou
key_works.what: Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback fails on reasoning tasks and can lower accuracy. It supports making an external checker the only judge, which is what dawnr's kernels are.

key_works.title: Enchanting Program Specification Synthesis by Large Language Models using Static Analysis and Program Verification
key_works.who: Cheng Wen, Jialun Cao, Jie Su, Zhiwu Xu, Shengchao Qin, Mengda He, Haokun Li, Shing-Chi Cheung, Cong Tian
key_works.year: 2024 (CAV venue not confirmed on the page)
key_works.what: Static analysis decomposes the program so the LLM proposes specifications piece by piece, and candidates are validated by the prover each round to stop error accumulation; reports 79% of programs verified from synthesized specs, a 1.592x gain, and a real X509-parser case. The page names no prover or spec language, so no Frama-C result is claimed here.

key_works.title: Can Large Language Models Transform Natural Language Intent into Formal Method Postconditions?
key_works.who: Madeline Endres, Sarah Fakhoury, Saikat Chakraborty, Shuvendu K. Lahiri
key_works.what: Scores LLM-written postconditions on correctness and discriminative power; the abstract says they are 'generally correct and able to discriminate incorrect code' and catch 64 historical Defects4J bugs. The direct precedent for dawnr's rule that a spec must reject a faulty variant.

key_works.title: Towards Neural Synthesis for SMT-Assisted Proof-Oriented Programming
key_works.who: Saikat Chakraborty, Gabriel Ebner, Siddharth Bhat, Sarah Fakhoury, Sakina Fatima, Shuvendu Lahiri, Nikhil Swamy
key_works.what: About 600K lines of open F* code (about 32K top-level definitions; an extended 940K-line set). Each task is a type-directed synthesis judged by F*; fine-tuned Phi-2 and StarCoder compare favorably with GPT-4 at much lower cost, and type-based retrieval helps significantly. The direct prior art for dawnr's per-parameter claim in one prover, and it shares three authors with nl2postcond.

key_works.title: AlgoVeri: An Aligned Benchmark for Verified Code Generation on Classical Algorithms
key_works.who: Haoyu Zhao, Ziran Yang, Jiawei Li, Deyuan He, Zenan Li, Chi Jin, Venugopal V. Veeravalli, Aarti Gupta, Sanjeev Arora
key_works.what: 77 classical algorithms with identical functional contracts across Dafny, Verus and Lean; Gemini-3 Flash reaches 40.3% on Dafny, with Verus at 24.7% and Lean at 7.8% (model not stated), and iterative repair reportedly triples one model's Dafny rate. The authors say their numbers are not comparable to earlier suites. The closest matched-contract multi-prover design, but it measures per-prover success, not cross-prover acceptance.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Overlap: the generate, check, repair loop is not original to dawnr. Self-Debugging, AlphaVerus's Treefinement and AutoSpec's per-round validation already run that loop, and AlphaVerus bootstraps verified data through self-improving translation with a reward-hacking filter, which is the role dawnr's gate plays. Threat: the twin gate is a specific form of spec-adequacy checking that nl2postcond (postconditions must discriminate faulty code) and Clover (no false positives on adversarial incorrect programs) already establish as a concept, so dawnr cannot claim the concept itself; it can claim a hard seven-kernel gate with a measured error rate. Confirmation: Philipp 2026 shows that one verifier is not enough and that weak checks get gamed, which supports pairing the twin refutation with the problem's own tests, and Huang et al. support making the external checker the only judge. The per-parameter thesis is partly confirmed inside single provers: Chakraborty et al. report that fine-tuned Phi-2 and StarCoder compare favorably with GPT-4 on F* at much lower cost, and Goedel-Code-Prover reaches 62.0% at 8B in Lean. What remains distinctive is the multi-prover, twin-gated version, and it has to be measured as that. Industry threat: AWS already ships formal validation of LLM answers, but as policy logic in the cloud; dawnr's distinct claims are program-level proofs across seven kernels and offline operation. None of the twelve fetched works uses cross-prover agreement as an acceptance rule or reports what each added prover contributes.
opportunities: Marginal-kernel curve: on one candidate pool, report wrong-but-accepted rates at every agreement threshold from 1 to 7 kernels, with known-answer tests as ground truth. None of the fetched works reports per-prover marginal value, and Philipp 2026's finding that the prover alone missed defects is the motivating case.

Calibrated twin-gate error rate: plant known-weak specs and measure how many survive all seven twins. This is the adequacy analogue of nl2postcond's discriminative-power metric, but as a hard gate with a published miss rate.
Matched-contract benchmark across all seven kernels: vericoding and AlgoVeri each span three kernels, and none of the fetched works spans seven.

Shortcut audit: count admit, assume, sorry, axiom and similar escapes in accepted answers across the seven kernels. Philipp 2026 documents an agent bypassing checks while reporting success, so an automated escape detector is a checkable deliverable.

Matched-parameter test with three arms: raw code, single-kernel-verified survivors, and seven-kernel survivors at equal model size. Chakraborty et al. show small models compete in F* alone, so the cross-kernel gain is the open question, and the single-kernel arm is what attributes any gain to multi-kernel agreement rather than to verification alone.

Repair in the loop: dawnr's gate, as described, filters samples without repair. AlgoVeri reportedly sees iterative repair triple one model's Dafny rate, so a repair round fed by each kernel's own error messages is a cheap yield test, and it also shows whether kernel disagreements are repairable.
An offline, program-level verified assistant: the only industry precedent I fetched (AWS) is cloud and policy-logic, and none of the fetched works targets a local seven-kernel checker.
findings.direction_hint: Run one experiment first: the marginal-kernel curve together with the twin-gate miss rate. On the existing candidate pool, measure wrong-but-accepted rates for each agreement threshold from 1 to 7 kernels against known-answer tests, and separately measure how often planted weak specs survive all seven twins. The result either justifies the seven-kernel gate with numbers or shows which kernels add nothing, and it answers the question the fetched literature leaves open.

findings.dimension: Formal/external checking and selective prediction (abstention) against LLM hallucination, verified tool use, and checker-grounded code generation
findings.landscape: Checker-in-the-loop generation is now established: LLM-Modulo (ICML 2024) argues LLMs should propose while external verifiers decide, and single-verifier systems followed for Dafny (Clover; DafnyPro, Jan 2026, which reports 85.7% to 100% verification across four suites with Claude 3.7 Sonnet and blocks edits to the base program), Verus (AutoVerus, OOPSLA 2025, over 90% of 150 tasks; AlphaVerus, ICML 2025), and F* (ICSE 2025), with decode-time type constraints (PLDI 2025) and tool-critique loops (CRITIC, ICLR 2024) alongside. The bottleneck has moved to specifications and proofs: Verina (Lean, v3 March 2026) reports o3 at 72.6% correct code, 52.3% sound-and-complete specs and 4.9% verified proofs, and CLEVER (161 Lean problems) reports that its few-shot and agentic baselines all struggle to reach full verification. Abstention work is statistical rather than proof-based: Jeong et al. control the false discovery rate of selective code generation using generated unit tests (revised June 2026), a May 2026 distribution-free abstention rule for code (arXiv 2605.17029) uses execution consistency, and semantic entropy (Nature 2024) and conformal factuality (ICML 2024) trade coverage for reliability, so their truth signal is samples or tests, not proofs. Theory and product have converged on the same stance: Kalai and Vempala (STOC 2024) prove calibrated models must hallucinate on singleton arbitrary facts, Kalai et al. (arXiv 2509.04664, Sept 2025) argue that current grading penalizes uncertain responses, and AWS Automated Reasoning checks in Bedrock Guardrails (GA per current docs) return VALID, INVALID, TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS or TOO_COMPLEX while stating that VALID covers only what the policy variables capture. Package hallucination is measured at scale (at least 5.2% of suggested packages for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones, USENIX Security 2025), and this brief is partial: 23 searches completed before the session search cap blocked three more (vericoding, specification gaming, and 2026 abstention benchmarks), so 2026 coverage beyond CodeRefuser and DafnyPro is thin.

key_works.title: Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate
key_works.what: Statistical lower bound: calibrated LMs must hallucinate on arbitrary facts at a rate near the share of facts seen exactly once in training (Good-Turing), independent of architecture and even with error-free data; post-training is suggested for singleton facts, while repeated or systematic facts such as arithmetic lack this pressure.
key_works.who: Adam Tauman Kalai, Santosh S. Vempala

key_works.title: Why Language Models Hallucinate
key_works.what: Argues hallucination persists because training and benchmark grading reward confident guessing over admitting uncertainty; calls for rescoring widely used leaderboards rather than adding hallucination tests. The exact scoring rule is not confirmed from the abstract page.
key_works.who: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, Edwin Zhang

key_works.title: Task Abstention for Large Language Models in Code Generation
key_works.what: Calibrated abstention rule from multiple hypothesis testing that uses execution consistency, needs no oracle tests, and claims a distribution-free guarantee; the abstract reports only qualitative gains and names no error rate. A secondary summary calls the method CodeRefuser; the abstract page does not.
key_works.who: Yanke Zhou, Yuhao Tan, Senrong Xu, Zenan Li, Yuan Yao, Taolue Chen, Xiaoxing Ma

key_works.title: Towards Functional Correctness of Large Code Models with Selective Generation
key_works.what: Selective code generator abstains when generated unit tests cannot confirm functional correctness; guarantee controls correctness among non-abstained answers, which the abstract equates with false discovery rate control. Earlier arXiv title: Selective Code Generation for Functional Guarantees.
key_works.who: Jaewoo Jeong, Taesoo Kim, Sangdon Park

key_works.title: We Have a Package for You!
key_works.what: 576,000 code samples from 16 code LLMs in two languages; average share of hallucinated packages at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models; 205,474 unique hallucinated package names (figures as stated in the revised version the abstract page reflects).
key_works.who: Joseph Spracklen, Raveen Wijewickrama, A H M Nazmus Sakib, Anindya Maiti, Bimal Viswanath, Murtuza Jadliwala

key_works.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
key_works.what: Samples about 5 answers, clusters them by meaning (LLM judge or NLI), and computes entropy over clusters to flag confabulations; beats baselines on AUROC and AURAC across QA datasets and models; misses errors from consistently wrong training data or deception, and costs about 10x a single answer. Fetched via the authors' OATML post because the Nature page redirected to a login.

key_works.title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
key_works.what: Treats each output's entailment set as an uncertainty set and applies a conformal back-off that makes the output less specific until a high-probability correctness guarantee holds; reports 80-90% guarantees on FActScore, NaturalQuestions and MATH while keeping most of the original output (ICML 2024 venue from a search listing).

key_works.title: CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
key_works.what: Draft, check with external tools (a search engine for facts, a code interpreter for code), then revise from the critique; consistent gains on QA, math program synthesis and toxicity; the abstract page gives no numbers.
key_works.who: Zhibin Gou, Zhihong Shao, Yeyun Gong, Yelong Shen, Yujiu Yang, Nan Duan, Weizhu Chen

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.what: Checks consistency among generated Dafny code, its docstring and its annotations, combining formal verification with LLMs; up to 87% acceptance of correct CloverBench programs with zero false positives on adversarial incorrect ones; flagged 6 faulty programs in MBPP-DFY-50 (no rates reported for that set).
key_works.who: Chuyue Sun, Ying Sheng, Oded Padon, Clark Barrett

key_works.title: AutoVerus: Automated Proof Generation for Rust Code
key_works.what: LLM agents mirror expert proof phases (preliminary proof, refinement with generic tips, debugging from verifier error messages); correct proofs for over 90% of 150 Verus tasks; over half solved within 30 seconds or 3 LLM calls.
key_works.who: Chenyuan Yang, Xuheng Li, et al. (incl. Shan Lu, Shuvendu Lahiri)

key_works.title: AlphaVerus: Bootstrapping Formally Verified Code Generation through Self-Improving Translation and Treefinement
key_works.what: Translates programs into verified code, refines with tree search on verifier feedback, then screens out specifications and programs that do not match intent, described as preventing reward hacking; LLaMA-3.1-70B without fine-tuning. The abstract page gives no pass rates.
key_works.who: Pranjal Aggarwal, Bryan Parno, Sean Welleck

key_works.title: DafnyPro: LLM-Assisted Automated Verification for Dafny Programs
key_works.what: Inference-time framework: a diff-checker rejects any output whose program body differs from the base program, a pruner removes non-inductive invariants, and tactic hints are retrieved. Claude 3.7 Sonnet verifies 100% of Clover, 98.73% of MBPP-Dafny, 94.39% of HumanEval-Dafny and 85.67% of DafnyBench; the authors cite model edits to base code ('cheating') among factors in earlier DafnyBench results.
key_works.who: Debangshu Banerjee (UIUC; AWS internship), Olivier Bouissou (AWS), Stefan Zetzsche (AWS)

key_works.title: Automatic Generation of Formal Specification and Verification Annotations Using LLMs and Test Oracles
key_works.what: Adds Dafny pre- and postconditions, loop invariants and helpers in a verifier-feedback repair loop; test assertions act as oracles on the generated specs; 98.2% of 110 programs with a Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 mix within 8 repair rounds; proof helpers drive difficulty; the abstract does not report how tight the generated specs are.
key_works.who: Joao Pascoal Faria, Emanuel Trigo, Vinicius Honorato, Rui Abreu

key_works.title: Can Large Language Models Transform Natural Language Intent into Formal Method Postconditions?
key_works.what: Scores LLM postconditions for correctness and for bug-completeness, the fraction of LLM-generated or seeded mutants a postcondition kills (4 to 233 per EvalPlus problem, median 55); GPT-4 kills all mutants for up to 62.2% of problems (average completeness 0.85); 70 buggy methods from 64 Defects4J bugs; the authors note seeded bugs may inflate completeness.
key_works.who: Madeline Endres, Sarah Fakhoury, Saikat Chakraborty, Shuvendu K. Lahiri

key_works.title: Towards Neural Synthesis for SMT-Assisted Proof-Oriented Programming
key_works.what: About 600K lines and 32K top-level F* definitions framed as type-directed synthesis tasks, each candidate checked by querying F*; fine-tuned Phi-2 and StarCoder compare favorably with GPT-4 at far lower compute; type-based retrieval gives significant gains; the page gives no benchmark numbers.
key_works.who: Saikat Chakraborty, Gabriel Ebner, Siddharth Bhat, Sarah Fakhoury, Sakina Fatima, Shuvendu Lahiri, Nikhil Swamy

key_works.title: CLEVER: A Curated Benchmark for Formally Verified Code Generation
key_works.what: 161 Lean problems with two tasks: a specification compared with a held-out ground-truth spec, and an implementation proven against the spec; avoids test supervision, LLM-written annotations, and leaking or vacuous specs; all tested few-shot and agentic methods struggle to reach full verification.
key_works.who: Amitayush Thakur, Jasper Lee, George Tsoukalas, et al. (incl. Swarat Chaudhuri)

key_works.title: VERINA: Benchmarking Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.what: 189 curated Lean tasks scoring code, specification and proof separately and jointly; best model (o3, v3) at 72.6% correct code, 52.3% sound-and-complete specs and 4.9% verified proofs; authors name proof generation as the main bottleneck.
key_works.who: Zhe Ye, Zhengxu Yan, Jingxuan He, Timothe Kasriel, Kaiyu Yang, Dawn Song

key_works.title: Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
key_works.what: Organizes abstention methods, benchmarks and metrics along query, model and human-values axes; open questions include a task-general abstention ability; the abstract page does not say whether code or formal verification is covered.
key_works.who: Bingbing Wen, Jihan Yao, Shangbin Feng, Chenjun Xu, Yulia Tsvetkov, Bill Howe, Lucy Lu Wang

key_works.title: Type-Constrained Code Generation with Language Models
key_works.what: Masks decoding tokens that would break typing rules (prefix automata with a search over inhabitable types), with a claimed sound well-typedness guarantee; compile errors reduced by more than half on HumanEval and MBPP, with functional gains across open-weight models above 30B; formal core is a simply typed language, TypeScript the practical test.
key_works.who: Niels Mundler, Jingxuan He, Hao Wang, Koushik Sen, Dawn Song, Martin Vechev

key_works.title: Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
key_works.what: Position paper: auto-regressive LLMs cannot plan or self-verify on their own, so they should generate candidates in a bi-directional loop with external model-based verifiers; no experiments.
key_works.who: Subbarao Kambhampati, Karthik Valmeekam, Lin Guan, Mudit Verma, Kaya Stechly, Siddhant Bhambri, Lucas Paul Saldyt, Anil B Murthy

key_works.title: Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (AWS user guide)
key_works.what: Formal-logic validation of natural-language answers against a policy built from source documents; verdicts include VALID, INVALID, TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS and TOO_COMPLEX; detect mode only; generally available in six regions, English only; a VALID result covers only statements captured by policy variables (its example: a fake doctor's note can pass if no variable captures it); the docs give no accuracy figure. The April 2025 AWS ML blog described the preview.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Part of dawnr is not original, so the claim has to move. Checker-gated generation (an LLM proposes, a formal checker must accept before the answer is kept) has prior art in LLM-Modulo, Clover, AutoVerus, AlphaVerus, DafnyPro, Faria et al. (2026) and the F* synthesis work, so dawnr cannot claim the idea itself. The twin-refutation adequacy gate also has precedent: nl2postcond (FSE 2024) scores LLM postconditions by the mutants they kill, and SpecGen (ICSE 2025, search-only, not fetched) uses mutation operators on candidate annotations; dawnr's one-edit twin refuted at a concrete input is the same family in a deterministic, per-row, per-kernel form, so the defensible claim is that form plus multi-kernel agreement. The honest-refusal rule is confirmed by theory: Kalai and Vempala (STOC 2024) show calibrated models must hallucinate on singleton arbitrary facts, and Kalai et al. (2025) argue that current grading penalizes uncertain responses and should be rescored, the same ordering as dawnr's rule. The gap is measurement and statistics: the selective-prediction works (Jeong et al., CodeRefuser, conformal factuality, semantic entropy) report coverage against error with guarantees, the brief shows no coverage-versus-false-verdict curve for t, and their truth signal is tests or samples where dawnr's is proofs, which is stronger but harder to scale. In the works fetched, none uses agreement across several independent kernels, the design element that looks unclaimed. The residual risk is spec-intent mismatch: AWS's VALID covers only what the policy variables capture (its example: a fake doctor's note can pass if no variable captures it), and Verina's 52.3% sound-and-complete rate for o3 says mis-specification is common. The twin gate checks that a spec is strong enough to refute one edit, not that it states the intended property, so that check falls to the problem's own tests and to reference-spec comparison. Industry threats: AWS already sells a managed formal verdict for LLM answers (its docs give no accuracy figure; a secondary summary's 99% figure is unverified), and Harmonic markets Lean-checked outputs as hallucination-free (secondary report, not fetched); both target policies or mathematics rather than program code.
opportunities: Publish a coverage-versus-false-verdict curve for t with three-state verdicts (verified; refuted by a kernel or the twin; unverifiable, with the reason), scoring refusals apart from wrong answers as the Kalai et al. (2025) argument recommends, and report it next to pass rate on the same problems.

Treat cross-kernel disagreement as an abstention signal: when kernels split on one program (one proves, another times out or rejects), count it as unverifiable and measure how often a split flags a bad row. In the works fetched, each system uses one verifier, so agreement across kernels looks unclaimed.

Measure the spec-intent gap on accepted rows: compare each accepted spec with a hand-written reference spec on a held-out sample (CLEVER-style equivalence) and score mutant completeness per row (nl2postcond-style), to estimate the rate of verified-but-wrong answers.

Give locallm refusal-labelled training targets: verifier-derived 'cannot verify' examples whose stated reason is the failing kernel and a counterexample. The abstention methods fetched learn from confidence, sampling or unit-test agreement, not from proof outcomes.

Move one check to decode time in the teacher pipeline: t's type system as a token mask (type-constrained decoding cut compile errors by more than half on HumanEval and MBPP) would discard fewer teacher samples before the proof stage. Monitor-guided decoding (NeurIPS 2023, search-only, not fetched) is the static-analysis precedent.
Borrow DafnyPro's diff-guard for the proof stage: reject any output whose program body differs from the base program, so proof hints cannot be bought by editing the program.

For the offline CLI, check every suggested dependency against a lockfile or registry mirror before offering an install, since 5.2% to 21.7% of suggested packages were hallucinated in Spracklen et al. This is a cheap verified tool a coding assistant can ship.
findings.direction_hint: Make the seven-kernel gate a measured selective predictor: publish coverage-versus-false-verdict curves with three-state verdicts (verified, refuted by a kernel or the twin, unverifiable with reason), then run a head-to-head on the same problems against a consistency-based abstention baseline (a Jeong et al.-style FDR selector or semantic entropy). The test is whether cross-kernel agreement lowers false verdicts at matched coverage, a comparison none of the works fetched makes.

findings.dimension: Formal methods + AI for safety-critical and autonomous/flight software (SPARK/Ada, DO-178C/DO-333, ML assurance, PX4 verification, verified controllers; market and regulatory pull)
findings.landscape: Regulators are converging on process-based assurance for AI rather than proof: EASA's AI Roadmap 2.0 has produced a rulemaking NPA (2025-07, Level 1-2 AI; trade-press report, not fetched) and Concept Paper Issue 03 (proposed 3 June 2026, comments closed 12 August 2026, now also covering Level 3, reinforcement learning and symbolic AI), while the FAA's first-iteration roadmap (2024) sets principles (learned vs. learning AI, incremental path, designer accountability) and the trade-press account names no formal method. The standards to build against are still in flight: per a search snippet of an August 2025 deck I could not read, ED-324/ARP6983 (SAE G-34/EUROCAE WG-114) targeted June 2026 publication; ISO/PAS 8800:2024 covers AI in road vehicles and treats training and evaluation data as safety items (ISO page returned 403); and EU AI Act Annex I high-risk duties are reported, from secondary sources only, to move to 2 August 2028. DO-333 is the sanctioned formal-methods route, but its public certification record is thin (the clearest account I found is a 2017 AdaCore-authored piece saying no program had claimed credit yet), and I found no 2025-26 flight-software proof case study. Research and product signals are strongest for LLM-plus-verifier pipelines: AutoVerus (OOPSLA 2025) generates correct Verus proofs for over 90% of a 150-task suite, Marmaragan (arXiv, Feb 2025) gets 50.7% of SPARK annotations right with GPT-4o on a curated set, and AWS shipped Automated Reasoning checks in Bedrock Guardrails (GA 6 Aug 2025, vendor-stated 'up to 99%' accuracy) that check LLM answers against formal policy logic. Funding is moving toward tooling: ARIA's 59m GBP Safeguarded AI programme, after dated updates from November 2025 to May 2026, now centres on an open-source toolkit for AI-produced formally verified artefacts and no longer mentions world models or safety specifications. PX4 formal work is thin: a 2020 requirement-level model check of PX4 return and collision-avoidance behaviour (search snippet, checker unnamed), runtime monitoring, and PGFuzz (NDSS 2021, 156 bugs across ArduPilot, PX4 and Paparazzi from 56 temporal-logic policies); I found no 2025-26 proof-based PX4 flight-logic result. Coverage is incomplete because the WebSearch budget ran out after about 20 searches, so verified-controller work (KeYmaera X/VeriPhy-style), Ferrocene or Rust qualification, and mutation-based specification adequacy were not searched.

key_works.title: Towards Guaranteed Safe AI: A Framework for Ensuring Robust and Reliable AI Systems
key_works.what: Position paper: guaranteed-safe AI = world model + safety specification + verifier that emits an auditable certificate; argues the main alternative assurance approaches are inadequate. The closest published statement of dawnr's premise (certificate-first), minus the world model that physical autonomy claims need.

key_works.title: Minimize AI hallucinations and deliver up to 99% verification accuracy with Automated Reasoning checks (AWS, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails)
key_works.what: Shipped product: an uploaded natural-language policy becomes formal rules, and LLM answers are checked by formal logic with ambiguity flags; GA 6 Aug 2025 in US and EU regions at launch; 'up to 99%' accuracy is vendor-stated with no method given. Sold per text processed, so a market exists for LLM-plus-formal-check, but it is cloud-only and aimed at enterprise policy text, not code.

key_works.title: AutoVerus: Automated Proof Generation for Rust Code
key_works.what: Agent network that writes Verus proofs, refines them with generic tips, and repairs them from verifier errors; over 90% of a 150-task suite solved, over half within 30 s or three LLM calls. The closest precedent for dawnr's LLM-plus-verifier loop, in Rust rather than t.
key_works.who: Yang et al. (13 authors incl. Microsoft Research)

key_works.title: Verifying LLM-Generated Code in the Context of Software Verification with Ada/SPARK (Marmaragan)
key_works.what: GPT-4o drafts SPARK annotations for existing Ada programs; correct on 50.7% of a curated benchmark with annotations removed. The Ada/SPARK precedent for the LLM-writes-the-proof step; a preprint, not peer-reviewed in the fetched record.
key_works.who: Cramer and McIntyre (names from search listing)

key_works.title: Safeguarded AI programme (ARIA)
key_works.what: 59m GBP programme whose own dated updates (Nov 2025 to May 2026) moved it to an open-source assurance toolkit for AI-produced verified artefacts plus cybersecurity applications; the page no longer mentions world models or safety specifications. A possible funder or peer for dawnr's tooling.
key_works.who: ARIA (UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency)

key_works.title: EASA releases latest issue of its Concept Paper on Artificial Intelligence for comment
key_works.what: Proposed Issue 03 (3 June 2026; comments due 12 Aug 2026) is the final concept-paper deliverable under AI Roadmap 2.0; adds Level 3 (advanced automation), reinforcement learning and symbolic AI to the Level 1-2 guidance of Issues 01-02.

key_works.title: FAA lays out 'roadmap' for AI safety in aircraft
key_works.what: FAA first-iteration roadmap as reported by a trade article (the FAA document itself was not read): seven principles including the learned vs. learning AI split and designer accountability; the report names no formal method and no planned policy statement.
key_works.who: FAA (reported by Military & Aerospace Electronics, 15 Aug 2024)

key_works.title: Guidance on the Assurance of Machine Learning in Autonomous Systems (AMLAS)
key_works.what: Safety-case patterns plus a lifecycle process for building ML assurance evidence into autonomous-system safety cases; the template dawnr's gates would have to map onto for any aviation or automotive buyer.
key_works.who: Hawkins, Paterson, Picardi, Jia, Calinescu, Habli (York group)

key_works.title: PGFUZZ: Policy-Guided Fuzzing for Robotic Vehicles
key_works.what: Fuzzes ArduPilot, PX4 and Paparazzi against 56 temporal-logic safety policies: 156 previously unknown bugs, 106 accepted by developers. The strongest public precedent for policy-as-specification on PX4, but it finds violations by testing and gives no proof.

key_works.title: The 6th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2025): Summary and Results
key_works.what: Neural-network verifier competition summary: 8 teams, 16 regular and 9 extended benchmarks, equal-cost AWS hardware, standard ONNX/VNN-LIB formats. Abstract only, so winners and per-benchmark results were not checked.

key_works.title: Artificial Intelligence Quantified (AIQ)
key_works.what: DARPA program testing whether mathematical foundations can predict and guarantee AI capabilities; partners NIST and the Department of War; program manager Patrick Shafto. The clearest government funding signal for quantitative AI guarantees I found; start date not on the page.

key_works.title: ISO/PAS 8800:2024, road vehicles: safety and AI
key_works.what: Publicly Available Specification for AI in series-production road vehicles; sits on ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 and adds an ML lifecycle; treats training, validation and evaluation data as safety items. Details from a UL write-up and store listings; the ISO page returned HTTP 403.

key_works.title: ED-324 / ARP6983 (ML development and assurance guidance for aviation)
key_works.what: Process standard for developing and certifying ML in aviation products (SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114). An August 2025 deck targeted June 2026 publication, but the deck was unreadable on fetch, so status is unconfirmed.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Confirmation: the guaranteed-safe-AI premise (a world model, a safety specification and a verifier that emits an auditable certificate) and AWS's shipped formal check of LLM answers both confirm the market and research premise that an AI answer should count only when a checker certifies it; dawnr's rule that an unverified answer is refused rather than trusted is the same stance in product form. Prior art that makes part of dawnr unoriginal: 'LLM writes the proof, verifier judges, agent repairs' is established for Verus (AutoVerus) and now for SPARK (Marmaragan), so the verifier loop alone is not novel; what remains distinct in dawnr is the conjunction of seven independent kernels, a one-edit twin refutation as the adequacy gate, and verified-only training rows. Boundary: dawnr specifies programs, not the physical world, so it lacks the world model the guaranteed-safe framing needs for autonomy claims; it can support code-level flight-software properties but not 'the drone will not crash' claims. Threat: as far as the standards' structure goes (DO-178C, DO-333, ED-324, AMLAS are not fetched here), certification credit comes from qualified tools, traceable evidence and a safety case rather than from cross-prover agreement as such, so the seven-kernel result is extra assurance evidence a regulator would have to weigh, not a route to credit. Market pull is real but slow: the aviation and automotive standards are 2024-2026 documents, and buyers will ask for an assurance case before any tool credit.
opportunities: An AMLAS-style assurance case for dawnr's verified-data pipeline: map the proof gate, twin refutation, held-out audit and refusal onto claims, arguments and evidence. I found no public write-up of a formally verified training-data pipeline in this form; AMLAS (arXiv:2102.01564) is the method to adopt.

Measured specification adequacy: report how often the one-edit twin catches too-weak specifications, and compare against PGFuzz-style policy-violation search and standard mutation testing. The mutation-adequacy literature was not searched, so whether this baseline is already published is unconfirmed.

A code-level PX4 case study rather than a physical-safety claim: a t spec of one flight-stack predicate (sensor validity or a failsafe transition) proved in all seven kernels, with the twin modelling a known bug class. PGFuzz finds violations by fuzzing without proof, so the artifact complements it rather than replicating it; any PX4 filing stays under the user's direction.

Verified floating-point control steps: the Rocq/Flocq float gate sits next to VCFloat (Coq, CompCert plus Flocq) and Boldo's Flocq work. An end-to-end t float step with stated error bounds did not appear in the results I saw, which surfaced only older work.

Cross-kernel disagreement as evidence: quantify how often independent kernels disagree on a real specification or soundness error, the kind of independence argument safety assessors ask about. I found no safety-critical paper measuring this, but the search was limited.

An offline, per-claim certificate checker for the CLI product: AWS's Automated Reasoning checks are a cloud guardrail for enterprise policy text, so an offline checker that emits a certificate per answer occupies a different slot. Check demand before building.
findings.direction_hint: Write one AMLAS-style argument for a code-level, PX4-relevant t module (for example a sensor-validity or failsafe-transition predicate, deliberately not a physical-safety claim): state the claims, cite the seven proofs as evidence and the one-edit twin refutation as the adequacy argument, and check whether the twin gate rejects a weakened version of the predicate that PGFuzz-style fuzzing shows is violable.

findings.dimension: Cross-checker trust: translation validation, proof-carrying code and certificate checking, independent re-checking across proof kernels, soundness bugs in verifiers and solvers, and multi-prover consensus
findings.landscape: Cross-checking is now the standard answer to 'who checks the checker', and 2024-2026 work takes three forms. LLM output is gated by an independent formal checker: LLM-Vectorizer (CGO 2025) uses Alive2, a bounded translation validator for LLVM IR, as its final check and reports 38.2% of vectorizations verified on TSVC, while a University of Waterloo preprint (Trivet) pairs LLMs with Lean and verifies or refutes 147 of 148 LLVM transformations, with every successful verdict re-checked by the Lean kernel. Certificates and independent kernels are maturing: Carcara (TACAS 2023) checks Alethe SMT proofs against the original problem, lean-smt (CAV 2025) reconstructs solver proofs as native Lean proofs, Lean4Lean is an external Lean 4 typechecker that found and fixed one soundness bug, and MetaRocq verifies a checker for a PCUIC model of Rocq under a strong-normalization postulate; witness validation (Witnesses 2.0, SPIN 2024) institutionalizes independent re-checking of verifier verdicts and documents how ambiguous semantics let validators confirm invalid or refute valid witnesses. The weak link is the solvers: CAST (PLDI 2026 student research competition) reports 12 soundness bugs among 42 found in Z3 and cvc5 over a 90-day run and 46 to date, and Verus's guide lists verifying the verifier and the Rust/LLVM compilers as out of scope. Coverage limit: the shared session web-search budget ran out after 13 searches from this run, so Lean, Rocq, Dafny and F* kernel bug studies were not searched, and the classic translation-validation and proof-carrying-code papers (Pnueli et al. 1998; Necula 1997 and 2000) are named from memory, not fetched.

key_works.title: LLM-Vectorizer: LLM-based Verified Loop Vectorizer
key_works.what: Test-guided multi-agent LLM vectorizes scalar loops; Alive2 (bounded translation validation for LLVM IR) is the formal check, and the abstract reports 38.2% of vectorizations verified on TSVC with 1.1x-9.4x speedups. An LLM proposes and a formal checker disposes, with the check bounded.

key_works.title: LLVM Translation Validation Automated with Large Language Models and Lean (Trivet)
key_works.what: LLMs handle transformation-specific obligations inside generated proof scaffolds, deterministic obligations are discharged automatically, and every successful verdict is checked by the Lean kernel. Verifies or refutes 147 of 148 LLVM transformations, including 10 fixed-bitwidth cases where Alive2 times out; the unscaffolded baseline solved 26 fewer.

key_works.title: Enhancing Translation Validation of Compiler Transformations with Large Language Models
key_works.what: Runs Alive2 first; where Alive2 does not settle a transformation, fine-tuned LLM predictions decide which transformations get fuzzed for counterexamples. The abstract gives no accuracy figures and does not say how unresolved cases are reported. A contrast case for a refusal-first gate.

key_works.title: Carcara: proof checker and elaborator for SMT proofs in the Alethe format (TACAS 2023 paper and repository)
key_works.what: Independent checker for SMT proofs in Alethe format; a check takes the proof and the original SMT-LIB problem, and the tool can also elaborate proofs. The README confirms the TACAS 2023 paper but states no checking guarantee and no limitations.

key_works.title: Lean-SMT: An SMT tactic for discharging proof goals in Lean
key_works.what: Turns Lean goals into SMT problems and reconstructs the proof-producing solver's proof as native Lean proofs, so the Lean kernel checks the result. Authors claim a smaller trusted core 'without sacrificing too much performance' and evaluate on Sledgehammer's SMT benchmarks.

key_works.title: Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean
key_works.what: External typechecker for Lean 4 written in Lean, described as the first complete checker other than Lean's C++ reference. About 20-50% slower; reports one soundness bug found and fixed; correctness is proved for parts of the kernel only.

key_works.title: MetaRocq (Rocq formalized in Rocq)
key_works.what: Fuel-free verified reduction, conversion and type checker for PCUIC, proved correct and complete with respect to the PCUIC specification; the proof assumes a strong-normalization postulate for well-typed PCUIC terms. The page does not connect the verified checker to Rocq's OCaml kernel.

key_works.title: Mixing HOL and Coq in Dedukti
key_works.what: Uses Dedukti as a logical framework to translate HOL and Coq developments and combine them; the demo is a Coq sorting algorithm on HOL's naturals. The abstract says nothing about checking or trusting the translated proofs.

key_works.title: Aeneas: Rust Verification by Functional Translation
key_works.who: AeneasVerif (Ho and Protzenko, ICFP 2022 per Microsoft Research listing)
key_works.what: Translates a subset of safe Rust (via Charon into LLBC) into pure functional code for F*, Coq, HOL4 or Lean; unsafe code and concurrency are out of scope for now. The closest existing one-source, many-provers system to t's lowering.

key_works.title: Software Verification Witnesses 2.0
key_works.what: Verifiers can be wrong, so witnesses are re-checked by independent validators built on different techniques. The C semantics of the format is ambiguous and probably no validator fully implements it, so valid witnesses can go unconfirmed and invalid ones can be confirmed. Moves the format from GraphML to YAML; SV-COMP has a witness validation track since 2023. Text read from the downloaded PDF.

key_works.title: CAST: Continuous Fuzzing for SMT Solvers
key_works.what: Differential testing and type-aware mutation in CI. A 90-day run on CVC5 and Z3 found 42 bugs (12 soundness), 33 confirmed and fixed upstream; continued operation has found 46 bugs to date. The abstract does not cover proofs or proof checking.

key_works.title: Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
key_works.who: Sun, Sheng, Padon, Barrett (Stanford; VMware Research)
key_works.what: Checks consistency among generated code, docstrings and Dafny annotations, combining formal verification with LLMs. Reports up to 87% acceptance of correct CloverBench programs and zero false positives on the adversarial incorrect set tested; flags 6 incorrect programs in MBPP-DFY-50.

key_works.title: A benchmark for vericoding: formally verified program synthesis
key_works.what: 12,504 specifications: Lean 7,141, Dafny 3,029, Verus/Rust 2,334. Off-the-shelf LLMs reach 27% in Lean, 44% in Verus/Rust and 82% in Dafny, showing how far per-language yield differs for the same kind of task.

key_works.title: Verus guide
key_works.what: Names Z3 as the solver that receives Verus's verification conditions. Lists 'verify the verifier itself' and 'verify the Rust/LLVM compilers' among things Verus does not intend to do, so those components stay outside what Verus proves.

key_works.title: Dafny reference manual
key_works.what: Section 1 states that 'the verifier is powered by Boogie ... and Z3', which confirms Z3 as Dafny's backend. The rest of the manual was not read in this run.

key_works.title: SPARK 2014 / GNATprove repository
key_works.what: GNATprove 'will detect and use Z3, cvc5 and alt-ergo when available in PATH'; built on an AdaCore fork of Why3. The README says nothing on proof certificates or the trusted base.

key_works.title: Frama-C WP plugin documentation
key_works.what: Recommended external provers are Alt-Ergo, Coq, Z3 and CVC4, plus any Why3-supported prover; WP first simplifies obligations with its internal Qed prover. Confirms multi-prover dispatch and the shared Z3 dependence.

key_works.title: F* homepage
key_works.what: Describes 'proof automation based on SMT solving' without naming the solver. The typechecker is written in F* and bootstrapped from OCaml; the page cites a 2012 paper that certifies the typechecker in F*, with coverage of today's typechecker not stated.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Prior art, not novelty: 'one spec, many provers' already exists (Aeneas emits F*, Coq, HOL4 and Lean from Rust; Dedukti was used in 2015 to combine HOL and Coq developments; SPARK and Frama-C WP dispatch obligations to several provers), and LLM-plus-formal-checker loops are published (LLM-Vectorizer, Trivet, Clover, Vericoding). What I found no fetched precedent for is the conjunction: a seven-way all-must-agree gate, a one-edit twin that must be refuted at a concrete input, and a refusal rule on the data path. Confirmation: the failure dawnr's refusal rule guards against is the one witness validation documents (validators confirming invalid witnesses under ambiguous semantics), and the refusal rule is the opposite of Wang and Xie's design, where LLM predictions steer checking when Alive2 is inconclusive. Threat, and the direct answer to whether consensus raises or lowers trust: consensus raises trust against one prover's bug in its own encoding, but the seven are not seven independent trust roots. Five are SMT-based as their main discharge engine (Dafny, Verus, SPARK, Frama-C WP, F*), Z3 is named as a backend in four of them by the fetched docs, and CAST shows Z3 and cvc5 still yield soundness bugs; only Lean and Rocq make their main verdicts proof terms checked by their own kernels (lean-smt's reconstruction feeds Lean's kernel). A second common-mode failure is the t-to-X lowering: all seven are generated from one t program, so a lowering bug can make all seven agree on the wrong program, and none of the fetched works validates a multi-prover lowering this way. Yield is a third cost: on the same problems, joint acceptance cannot exceed the weakest prover's acceptance, and off-the-shelf rates differ widely (Vericoding: 27% Lean, 44% Verus, 82% Dafny). Net: state the claim as measured diversity with shared roots counted once, not as seven. Limit of this read: the mutation-based specification-adequacy literature (a separate dimension) was not checked.
opportunities: Validate the lowering: for each accepted t program, run the t reference interpreter and all seven lowered forms on the same concrete inputs and make any disagreement a blocking verdict. None of the fetched works does this for a multi-prover spec lowering.

Replay every concrete-input refutation in an independent interpreter and reject any refutation that does not reproduce; a counterexample is a ground fact that re-execution can check, which is cheaper than trusting the prover's refutation.

Measure effective independence: on a sample of t programs, record which provers fail together and which solver versions (Z3, cvc5, Alt-Ergo) each row used, count shared roots once, and publish the number per row.

Where a solver can emit a proof (cvc5 in Alethe format, checkable by Carcara), check it independently; keep the Lean path on lean-smt-style reconstruction so the Lean kernel, not the solver, carries the verdict.

Audit escape hatches in every lowering and fail the gate on any hit: Lean (sorry, axiom, native_decide, implemented_by), Rocq (Admitted, Axiom), Dafny (assume, verify-false attributes), F* (admit, assume), Verus (assume, external_body), SPARK (pragma Assume). These keywords come from general knowledge of each tool and were not re-fetched.

Publish a witness-style interchange for dawnr verdicts with a precise semantics document, so independent validators can disagree visibly; Witnesses 2.0 is the cautionary case of silent disagreement under ambiguous semantics.

Treat cross-prover disagreement as a soundness-bug oracle: the existing t corpus already runs through seven provers, a ready-made differential harness of the kind CAST runs continuously against Z3 and cvc5.
Report the per-prover pass rate on the same problems next to the joint rate, so the yield ceiling set by the weakest prover is visible rather than hidden inside the seven-way gate.

findings.dimension: Market and career signal: demand for verified-code and AI-formal-methods work, who is funding and hiring (cloud, crypto, defense, aerospace), grants and residencies, and what a dawnr plus PX4 portfolio signals
findings.landscape: Verified AI output became a venture category in 2025-2026: Harmonic (Aristotle, Lean 4) raised $100M at a reported near-$900M valuation in July 2025 and $120M at $1.45B in November 2025, and Axiom Math raised $200M in March 2026 at a reported valuation above $1.6B to prove whether code and other machine-generated outputs are correct, explicitly extending beyond mathematics to software. Public money is following: DARPA's expMath (solicitation HR001125S0010) names 13 university performers, held a March 2026 kickoff where Harmonic, Axiom, Principia Labs, Math Inc. and Logical Intelligence presented, and UK ARIA's Safeguarded AI Track 1 (blue teams, machine-checked proofs of key security properties) has a proposal cut-off of 31 October 2026. Philanthropy and crypto fund the verification ecosystem: the Renaissance Philanthropy and XTX Markets AI for Math Fund made 22 awards in 2026, several of them Lean projects, the Ethereum Foundation's verified zkEVM hub lists 42 grants across zkVM, EVM and proof-system verification, and NSF's Safe Learning-Enabled Systems program is archived with no successor. Hiring is narrower than the headlines: the formal-verification postings in search results were mostly SoC, IP and processor roles at Microsoft, NVIDIA and Qualcomm, while software-proof roles naming Dafny or Lean appeared only in search results (not fetched) at AWS automated reasoning and in Ethereum Foundation and crypto listings, and AWS's open-source Cedar language is verified against a Lean model that the Lean project says is about 10 times smaller than its Rust code. Caveats: the session's web-search budget ran out before Principia Labs and Logical Intelligence funding could be checked, and several dollar figures (Harmonic's IMO claim, the AI for Math Fund per-award cap, the Ethereum Foundation's $20M budget, Axiom's earlier seed) rest on search snippets I could not fetch.

findings.relation_to_dawnr: Confirmation: the funded market now sells dawnr's core premise. Harmonic sells Lean-checked proofs, Axiom says its Verified AI proves whether AI-written code is correct, DARPA expMath and ARIA both fund machine-checked AI work, and the Lean FRO roadmap makes independent kernel checking a trust priority. Threat and prior art: verifying AI-written code by proof to cut hallucination is no longer original to dawnr; it is the pitch behind $100M-plus rounds, so dawnr should not lead with that general claim. Where dawnr still differs, as far as the sources I fetched show: none describes a gate that requires seven independent proof systems to verify the program and refute a one-edit twin, and Lean's independent-checker push covers one prover, not agreement across seven. Career and portfolio signal (an inference, not a measured hiring rate): a PX4 contribution lands in the defense supply chain, since Dronecode's 2025 review names Firestorm, a military-drone maker that runs PX4 in its flight stack, while a machine-checked component lands in the Lean and cloud-verification market; a portfolio showing both is less common than either alone. SPARK/Ada remains the established defense and aerospace route (search snippets only; no named 2025-2026 defense contract found).
opportunities: Cross-prover agreement as the trust claim: the Lean-based products I read (Harmonic, Axiom, Cedar) each rest on one proof system, and Lean's roadmap keeps independent checking inside Lean; a published seven-kernel agreement report with twin refutation makes a claim none of the fetched sources make.

Offline, auditable verification for security-critical code: ARIA's Track 1 wants machine-checked proofs for production-grade security components, and defense UAS makers build on PX4; the fetched pages of the cloud-first players (Harmonic, Axiom, Pramaana) describe no offline option, an open gap for an offline CLI assistant (hypothesis; demand not measured).

A public spec-adequacy benchmark: ARIA asks blue teams to prove properties under stated threat models and assumptions, and a benchmark that scores whether a spec is strong enough (the twin test) answers that directly; the AI for Math Fund has funded benchmark work (BELLE).

Grant fit for a multi-prover open tool: the AI for Math Fund's 2026 slate is open Lean tooling (LeanExplore, Hydropus, TorchLean), so an open dawnr checker is an eligible frame, subject to the fund's terms, which I did not read in full.

Ethereum zkEVM verification as an outside second check: the verified-zkevm hub shows 42 grants across zkVM, EVM and proof-system verification; an independent prover checking a zkVM spec is a plausible contribution, but I found no call asking for multi-prover work (hypothesis).

Residency route: the AI for Math Summer Fellowship (search snippet only) is the one residency-shaped program found; its 2026 window had closed (snippet deadline 10 April), and a 2027 window was not confirmed.
findings.direction_hint: Build the next public dawnr milestone as a security-critical component verified under all seven kernels, with the twin-refutation gate released as a standalone checker, and submit it to ARIA's Safeguarded AI Track 1 before the 31 October 2026 14:00 GMT cut-off (17 days from 14 October), or to the following quarterly cycle if the component is not ready; position it as the cross-prover check for AI-written safety code rather than a rival to Harmonic and Axiom in single-prover mathematics.
